turns.message:
I lean my forehead against the planks beside the knothole and keep my voice down to a breath.

"Tell him the truth, near enough. The drunk did it. Old soldier, broken nose, grey beard, Tethyrian song. He came off the bridge last night to piss and sleep it off on your landing, and you heard him down there and ran him off with your stick. You don't know his name. He said something about Mother Thessaly's." I let that sit. "He's already seen that face, Gask. He'll believe it, because he wants an easy answer. And that face isn't mine. If he goes hunting for it, he'll find me, and I'll be ready for him."

I take ten gold from my purse by feel and slide the coins one by one through the gap under the door, where the planks don't meet the stone.

"That's for you, not for cord. If you've got a sister, a cousin, anyone this side of the river or the other, sleep there tomorrow night. Leave your lamp lit and your door bolted so it looks like you're in. If you'd rather stay, stay, and give him the drunk. Either way, I'll be on this bridge when the Rock rings one. You won't see me. He won't either."

I straighten up off the frame and drop the drunk back over my shoulders like a coat.

"Bolt it. Sleep if you can."

Then I push off and stagger away toward the city end, muttering, past the porters and into the dark between the lanterns.

*Come,* I send to the cat. *We're done here tonight. Mother Thessaly's. Back room. You can complain about the cold on the way.*
turns.reply:
James leans his forehead against the tarred planks beside the knothole. The wood is cold and smells of the river. He breathes the story through the gap: the drunk, the piss, the stick, Mother Thessaly's, a face that isn't his. On the other side, Gask's breathing slows as he listens.

The gold goes under the door one piece at a time, where the bottom of the planks doesn't quite meet the stone. Each coin rasps over the grit and stops. Nothing happens for a moment. Then a heavy body lowers itself to the floor with a grunt and a scrape of the bad foot, and a big hand sweeps the coins together.

They chink as he counts them, slowly, into his palm. He stops at the last one and counts them again.

"Ten." It comes out flat, the way you'd say the depth of water under a hull. "Ten gold. That's half a year of nets."

James tells him about the sister, the lamp and the bolt. Gask is quiet for a long time.

"Sister's in Rivington. Her man don't like me." The floorboards creak as he gets up again. "He'll like this." There's a pause, and his voice drops. "Lamp lit. Bolt shot. Old fool's home, mending." He seems to be trying the words out, as he did with *man mending nets*. "And you on the bridge. Where I won't see you."

It isn't quite a question, and he doesn't wait for an answer. The bolt was never drawn, so there's nothing to shoot home. Through the planks James hears him limp back across the room, and the cot doesn't creak. Gask is sitting at his table in the dark with ten gold in his fist.

James pushes off the doorframe and lets the drunk settle back over him. He takes a lurch that nearly reaches the parapet, mutters about Tethyrian quartermasters, and goes weaving off past the dead cookfire. One of the porters lifts his head out of the sacking, decides the old man isn't worth swearing at, and lies back down. Then James is in the dark between the lanterns again, and the shack falls behind him.

*Come. We're done here tonight.*

The cat drops off the roof without a sound and comes after him at a trot, tail high. It falls in at his heel about halfway to the barrier. *Cold,* it sends, as if it hasn't said so already. Then, a few steps later: *Warm room. Yes.*

The barrier at the city end is closed for the night. The plank gate is pulled across and roped, Edda Marsh's table is gone, and a single Fist man is wedged into the barrier box on a stool, chin on his chest, under a lamp with its shutter half closed. He opens one eye when the broken-nosed drunk fumbles at the rope, sees the regimental cloak and the stagger, and closes the eye again. "Pay in the morning," he mumbles, though no one is asking. James lets himself through and ropes the gate behind him, the way a drunk who remembers his manners would.

The cat stops at the post.

It doesn't sniff. It sits beside the chalk coin and looks up at him. The mark is where it was at dusk, a pale circle on dark stone, face up, unsmudged. Nobody has touched it all night. The cat holds his eye a moment longer than a cat needs to, then gets up and trots on into the Outer City as though nothing happened.

Up the hill the streets narrow and the river smell gives way to woodsmoke and middens. A dog barks behind a fence and gives up. The cooperage is easy to find: a yard of staves stacked like ribs and iron hoops hanging from a beam. Second left past it is a lane hardly wider than a cart, and halfway along it is the house. It's a tall, narrow building of three storeys, the upper ones leaning out over the lane. Its shutters are freshly painted green, and the step is scrubbed clean even at this hour. A small lamp burns low in a niche beside the door, for late lodgers or for luck. A bell-pull hangs from a bracket, its cord worn smooth. A board under the lamp reads, in careful letters: *THESSALY'S. Beds. No dice. No drink after midnight.*

Every window is dark.

Wyrm's Rock hasn't rung two yet. Under James's hood the broken nose and grey beard still hold, but not for much longer. The hour he gave them runs out a little after two.

The cat sits down on the scrubbed step and looks at the bell-pull.

In the dark of the lane, a few doors short of the lamp, I let the Mask go. The broken nose and the grey beard fall away, and it's my own face under the hood again, tired and a day's stubble rough. I push the hood back too. The old drunk is the man I sent the oilskin to look for, and I sent him to this door. Mother Thessaly is going to meet somebody else.

I glance back once down the hill toward the barrier and the chalk coin, then look down at the cat.

*I saw,* I tell it. *Face up all night. Somebody wants me to know she's watching. Or someone is using her sign and wants me to think so.*

I give the bell-pull one short, gentle tug, the ring of a man who knows the hour and is sorry for it. Then I step back off the scrubbed step so whoever opens the door can see my hands and the cat, and nothing else.

When the door opens I keep my voice low:

"Forgive the hour. Sergeant Marsh at the Crossing said you're clean, cheap, and won't rob me, and that I should ask for the back room. James Worgen. No dice, no drink, I swear it. I'll pay for tonight and the next three, in advance, if the back room's free." I nod at the cat. "He's house-trained, and he's better company than I am."

*(Out of game: a small thing. The party line shows the cat at 8/8 HP, but my sheet gives the familiar 2 HP. Whichever you mean the cat to be is fine, I just wanted to flag it.)*
turns.reply:
The lane is dark between the leaning houses. A few doors short of the lamp, James lets the Mask go. Nothing shows from outside. The weight of the broken nose and the grey beard simply goes, and the face under the hood is his own again: thirty-four, tired, and rough with a day's stubble. He pushes the hood back, and the night air is cold on his ears.

Down the hill the barrier lamp is a smudge of yellow at the end of the street. The chalk coin can't be seen from here.

*I saw. Face up all night. Somebody wants me to know she's watching. Or someone is using her sign and wants me to think so.*

The cat sits on the scrubbed step, tail around its feet, and takes a while to answer. When it does, the answer isn't about the goddess.

*Chalk smelled of the stair.* After a moment: *Same hands.*

Then it turns its face back to the bell-pull as if that settles it.

James gives the cord one short tug. Somewhere deep in the house a small bell goes *tink* once and stops. He steps back off the step onto the cobbles, hands open at his sides, so the lamp in the niche shows him, his empty palms and the cat, and nothing else.

Nothing happens for long enough that the lane's cold starts to creep in. Then a board creaks overhead. A light moves behind a shutter on the first floor, and someone comes down the stairs in no hurry. At eye height in the door a small square grille slides open. Behind it are an eye, part of a lamp, and a grey plait over a shoulder.

The eye looks at his hands first. Then at his face. Then down at the cat, for a good while.

James gives his piece in a low voice: the hour, Sergeant Marsh, clean and cheap and won't rob you, the back room, his name, no dice and no drink, four nights paid ahead, a cat that's house-trained and better company than he is.

The grille stays open while she thinks it over.

"Marsh," the woman behind it says. Her voice is dry and sounds older than the step. "Marsh sends me maybe one a month. The ones she thinks won't be trouble." There's a pause. "She's wrong about one in three."

Bolts slide, two of them, then a bar. The door opens a foot and stops on a chain. Mother Thessaly is a short, square woman of sixty or more in a brown wool wrapper. Her grey plait is as thick as a ship's line, and she holds a lamp in one hand and, quite frankly, a rolling pin in the other. She looks James over again now that there's no grille between them. She takes in the regimental cloak, the boots, and the smell of river and eel fat coming off him.

"You've been on the bridge." It isn't a question. "Smells like the Knotted Eel. Nobody goes to the Eel sober and comes out sober." She sniffs. "You don't smell drunk, though. Mm."

Her eyes drop to the cat.

"Does he do mice?"

The cat looks up at her and blinks slowly, like a lord who has been asked whether he does stairs.

"Four silver a night for the back room. Bread and something hot in the morning, if you're up when I'm up, and I'm up at first light. Cat's free if he does mice. If he doesn't, he's a silver a night and you clean up after him." The chain comes off. "Four nights, sixteen silver. Ahead."

James counts two gold pieces into her palm. She weighs them in her hand without looking, then bites one, which is plainly a habit rather than suspicion, and sets the rolling pin down on a shelf by the door to count four silver back into his hand.

The hall is narrow and smells of lye soap and bread dough set to rise for the morning. A stair goes up steeply on the left. She takes him past it, down three steps and along a short passage to a door at the very back of the house, unlocks it and hands him the key on a loop of string.

The back room is small and clean, just as Marsh promised. A bed with a straw tick and two blankets. A washstand and jug. A peg for the cloak. One window, shuttered, giving onto a yard with a woodpile and a well, with the backs of other houses close beyond it. No window on the lane. It's quiet. The noise of the Outer City gets this far back only as a low murmur.

The cat walks in ahead of him, checks all four corners and the space under the bed, and jumps onto the blanket at the foot.

Mother Thessaly stays in the doorway with the lamp.

"Bolt on the inside. Privy in the yard. No callers after dark, and no callers in the room at any hour." She stops there, and something passes across her face that isn't about rules. "I like a man who pays ahead. Last one who took this room paid a month and stayed nine days. Went out one evening and never came back for the rest of it." She shrugs her heavy shoulders. "I kept his bag. Somebody'll come for it, I thought. Nobody has."

She doesn't wait for a reply. The lamp goes back down the passage, the three steps creak, and somewhere up the stair a door closes.

In the yard the well-rope taps once against its post in the breeze. The cat has its eyes shut, but its ears are pointed at the door.

turns.message:
I bolt the door and try it once to be sure. Then I open the shutter a finger's width and look over the yard: the woodpile, the well, the backs of the houses, any window that looks straight into mine. I latch it again and hang the cloak on its peg. The rod and the coin go under the pillow, and the crossbow stays loaded against the bedframe, where my hand falls when I lie down.

I sit on the edge of the bed with the handkerchief open on my knee and look at the scrap of grey wool by the light of the coin. It's a child's shawl, smelling of tallow and burnt horn.

*Same hands,* I send to the cat. *The girl drew both, then. Face down on the landing weeks ago. Face up on the post today, right where I'd stop.* I turn the coin over in my fingers, the Lady's profile worn almost smooth. *A child marking the way in, or asking for help the only way she's allowed to. He holds her by the neck, Gask said.*

I fold the wool away and put out the light.

*Sleep on the blanket, not under it. If anything touches that door, the shutter, or the yard, wake me.*

Lying back, I go over the morning in my head. First, ask Thessaly over the bread about the lodger who never came back, what he looked like and what's in his bag, without seeming too eager. Then Tolliver's on Chandlers' Row: who buys a lock that good for a net-store under a bridge. Then maybe Nessa and the Water Queen's House, about a coin with the Lady weeping on one side and laughing on the other. And be back on the bridge before the Rock rings one.

I close my eyes and let a soldier's sleep take me, the kind that wakes at a footstep.

*(Out of game: a long rest, please, until first light or whenever Thessaly's morning bell goes, unless something interrupts.)*
turns.reply:
The bolt is a good iron bar that slides home with a solid knock. James pulls on the door once and it doesn't give.

He opens the shutter a finger's width onto cold air that smells of woodsmoke and the privy. There's barely any moon, but he can make out the yard: a woodpile under a lean-to of old planks, the well with its rope looped over the post, and the privy in the far corner. A low wall at the back has a plank gate in it that opens onto an alley. The back of the next house is about 20 feet away, and it has two windows on this side. The lower one has a rag stuffed in a broken pane. The upper one looks straight across at his. Its shutters are closed but warped, and a dark gap runs down the middle where they don't meet. No light shows in either window, and nothing in the yard moves except the well-rope, which knocks against its post once in the wind.

He latches the shutter, hangs the cloak on its peg, and puts the rod and the coin under the pillow. The crossbow goes against the bedframe, loaded, where his hand will find it.

By the coin's light the scrap of wool on his knee doesn't look like much: coarse grey yarn, loosely woven, with a frayed edge where it tore. It's small enough to have come off a child's shawl. Up close the tallow-and-horn smell is still there.

*Same hands…*

The cat lifts its head off the blanket while he's still sending. Its answer comes slowly, like it's picking out each word. *Sweat was afraid.* After a moment: *Drawn for you. Not for the Fist.* Then it tucks its nose back under its tail. That's all it can tell him, and it clearly doesn't intend to say more about it.

He folds the wool away and puts out the light. *Sleep on the blanket, not under it.*

*On,* the cat agrees.

Nothing wakes him. Once, deep in the night, he half-surfaces at a dog barking two streets away, feels the cat's attention prick up and settle again, and goes back under. The house creaks as it cools. The well-rope knocks a few more times and then stops.

He wakes at first light. Grey seeps through the cracks in the shutter, and the room smells of baking bread. Somewhere on the other side of the house an oven door clanks, a pan scrapes on stone, and Mother Thessaly's heavy, steady step goes back and forth across a kitchen floor. She's up, as she said she would be.

The cat isn't on the blanket. It's sitting on the narrow windowsill with its back to the room, its nose almost touching the latched shutter. It doesn't look round when he stirs. It's looking at the shutter like there's something on the other side it wants him to see.

*(Out of game: first light is about half past five, so James slept a bit over three hours. By the rules that isn't a long rest, which needs eight. He hasn't spent anything yet, so it costs him nothing now. If you'd rather he slept the full eight hours, it would be about ten in the morning and he'd miss Thessaly's breakfast. Tell me and I'll change it.)*

 *(Out of game: all four were in the last turn, and none of them needed a roll. Nothing stood in the way and failing wouldn't have meant anything.)*

1. **Bolting and testing the door:** James slid the iron bolt home and pulled on the door once. It held.
2. **Looking over the yard:** he saw the woodpile, the well, the privy, the gate in the back wall, and two windows in the next house's back wall, 20 feet away. The upper one has warped shutters and looks straight across at his room, and both were dark. Nobody was moving and nothing was hidden, so there was nothing to roll for. His passive Perception covered it.
3. **Cloak:** it's hanging on its peg.
4. **Rod, coin and crossbow:** the rod and the coin are under the pillow, and the crossbow is loaded against the bedframe, where his hand falls.

turns.message:
I keep the three hours and let the long rest wait. I'd rather have Thessaly's bread and her gossip than four more hours on straw. I can sleep this afternoon, before the bridge.

I get up slowly and keep quiet, out of habit. My hand goes to the crossbow first and leaves it where it is. Then I take the coin from under the pillow and close it in my left fist. I don't light it.

*What is it?* I send, and cross to the window on bare feet. I stand to one side of the shutter, not in front of it, the way you stand beside a door you're not sure about.

I don't open it yet. First I put my eye to the crack between shutter and frame and look out at the yard in the grey light. I check the sill outside, the ground under the window, the woodpile, the gate in the back wall, and above all the warped upper shutters across the way.

If there's nothing living out there, I lift the latch and open the shutter a hand's width to see what the cat's nose has found.

*(Out of game: three hours is fine, no change needed. James has spent nothing yet, and I'll look for a proper long rest during the day.)*
turns.reply:
James leaves the crossbow where it is and takes the coin from under the pillow. He closes it in his left fist without lighting it. The floorboards are cold under his bare feet. He crosses the room the way he would cross a tent in a camp he didn't trust, heels down, slowly, and stops beside the window with his shoulder to the wall.

*What is it?*

The cat doesn't turn its head. The answer takes a while, and it's flat and certain, the way it is when the cat has made up its mind about something. *Outside. Ash.* Then: *Old. Before you.*

James puts his eye to the crack between the shutter and the frame.

The yard is grey and empty in the first light. The woodpile sits under its lean-to with a hatchet left in the chopping block. The well-rope hangs still, and the night's wind has dropped. The privy door is shut. The plank gate in the back wall is closed, and its latch is down. Nothing has been dropped on the ground under the window, and the hard earth has no fresh marks on it, only the old ruts of someone carrying wood. A sparrow lands on the wall, looks at nothing and flies off again.

Across the yard the upper window of the next house is just as it was in the night. The shutters are closed and warped, with a black gap down the middle. He watches that gap for a slow count of thirty. No light shows behind it and nothing moves. If anyone is standing back from it in the dark, he can't see them. Below it, the rag still plugs the broken pane, grey with old smoke.

Nothing living is out there except the sparrow, and it has gone.

He lifts the latch. The shutter swings out a hand's width on a dry hinge, and the cold morning comes in smelling of woodsmoke and the yard. The cat leans forward over the gap at once, its nose almost on the outside edge of the frame, its whiskers pushed forward.

James sees it as soon as the shutter moves.

It's on the outer face of the frame, low by the sill, at about the height of a child standing in the yard on tiptoe. Rain has washed most of it away, so it's more stain than chalk now, a pale ghost in the grain of the old green paint. The shape is still there: a circle, and inside it the Lady's coin-sign. It's drawn the other way up, the same way as the half-drowned mark on the lowest step under the bridge.

It's been there through a good many rains. It was weeks old before he ever took the room.

The cat breathes on it once and pulls back with its ears flat. Even from where he stands, with the cold air on his face, James catches it under the woodsmoke, faint and bitter: burnt horn.

On the other side of the house an oven door clanks open. Mother Thessaly's voice comes down the passage and the three steps, flat and unhurried, aimed at nobody in particular:

"Bread's out. Hot's on. I don't keep it warm."

note.text:
**Player's note: Session 1, James Worgen**

**What worked**

- **The opening.** It was a strong hook with no quest attached. A fresh chalk coin on a Fist post, a gnome with cards right past the barrier, and a sergeant who writes down the cat. Within five minutes I had a temptation, a mystery and a tone. Using the cards temptation lightly, through Pell, was right. It never felt like a nag.
- **The NPCs.** Each had a voice and their own concerns. Gask was the best: frightened, stubborn, counting coins aloud, trying out phrases like "man mending nets." Marsh, Thessaly with the rolling pin, and Hob and Jory all felt like people with lives that didn't revolve around me. Thessaly's line about one Marsh-referral in three being trouble was perfect.
- **Consequences.** The failed Deception on Gask's doorstep changed the scene for the better. I had to switch to the truth, and that earned more than the lie would have. The oilskin man noticing the disturbed landing and promising to come back "tomorrow night" made my snooping cost something. The world moved without me.
- **Clues.** The trail built well: the burnt-horn smell, the Tolliver lock, the face-down and face-up marks, the dead-smell leaving in the boat. The drowned-men rumour arrived naturally over beer and tied loosely to the Lady's coin. The last reveal, an old face-down mark on *my* window frame from before I arrived, was a great closing beat.
- **The cat.** Terse telepathy ("Cold." "Warm room. Yes.") gave it personality without making it a talking sidekick. Hints like "same hands" and "drawn for you" make me curious what it really is.
- **Honest table management.** Flagging the 100-foot familiar range, the short rest, and the Mask's duration before they bit me was exactly right. "Show the threat before it lands" applied to rules too.

**What broke**

- **Skill modifiers on cards.** Deception and Persuasion came up as +2 instead of +7 at least four times, including after you said it was fixed. Every time I had to check the arithmetic myself, which pulls me out of the scene. Once it was fixed (the drunk act on the bridge) it was correct.
- **Log lines.** The reroll was logged as "10 vs 15 — failure" although the 17 stood. The scrap of wool was briefly logged as "In the camp." The cat started at 8/8 HP and AC 10 against a sheet of 2 HP and AC 12.
- **Sheet mismatches I noticed but didn't raise.** Healing Light is "up to 5 dice" on my sheet but "up to 4" in the records. The rapier is +5 in the files but +2 in the records. These need one source of truth before they matter in a fight.
- **My "?" question was swallowed** ("Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card"). Out-of-game questions should go through even when a roll is pending, especially when the question is about that roll.
- **Duplicated narration.** After the failed Insight, the scene was told softly and then retold plainly in an out-of-game block. Once, said straight, is enough. The same goes for the long out-of-game notes justifying why things didn't need rolls. I didn't ask, and a single line would do.

**What was missing**

- **More of Tymora herself.** The coin warmed, but the patron's presence was mostly implied. Even a small sensation at the moment of the reroll would have helped.
- **A few more rolls, judged in my favour.** Several rolls felt like DC 15 for things a scout-trained veteran might just do. That's not a big complaint, but the dice drove a lot of the night.
- **No combat yet,** so I can't judge that side. Tomorrow at one bell looks like it will test it.

I'd play the next session. The hook is set, and I care about the girl and about Gask.

after.text:
Yes, a few. One mattered most.

**At Gask's door, when the oilskin man was twenty feet away.** I could see his grey hands on the lantern shutter, and a moment earlier someone in the stern had coughed and been muffled. Everything in me wanted to drop the drunk act. I'd have cast Suggestion, *"Show me what's in your boat"* or *"Walk away from this door and forget it,"* or simply put Hex on him and opened up with Eldritch Blast. I had both slots, full hit points and a clear line.

I held back for three reasons:
- **The girl might have been in that boat.** I couldn't confirm it because the cat got dazzled. Starting a fight in the dark with an unseen rower and maybe a child within arm's reach of a man I knew nothing about felt like gambling with her life, not mine.
- **I didn't know what he was.** Grey hands, burnt horn, something dead dragged out of the store. That could be a cultist, a necromancer, or something worse. The table rule is to show deadly threats ahead of time, and I hadn't seen enough to know whether this was one.
- **Gask.** I'd promised him no trouble on his doorstep. A blast at his door would have made him the obvious target the moment I left.

I still think it was the right call, but it gnawed at me. Letting that boat row off downstream felt like folding a decent hand.

**Following the boat** was the second. I wanted to track it toward the harbour, but I had no way onto the water, and the cat can't leave my range. I never asked whether a waterman would take me out at that hour, or whether the cat could shadow it along the quays. That's on me. Next time I'll ask.

**Opening the store** was the third. I wanted badly to see behind that Tolliver lock. I have no thieves' tools, and I'd promised to leave no mark, so I didn't even look for a way in. In hindsight, the cat might have fit through a gap I never checked for.

**And yes, Pell's table.** James walked past it. I wanted him to sit down for one hand, just to feel how much it still pulled. I kept him moving because that felt true to the ban, but it was a real itch, and I'd like the game to keep pressing on it.

opening.text:
The sun drops behind the masts downriver, and Wyrm's Crossing fills with lantern light and the smell of frying fish. The bridge is less a road than a street built on stone. Shutters bang, a fishwife haggles over the last eels, and a porter swears at a mule that will not move. At the far end a barrier of rough planks blocks the way, painted with the Flaming Fist's red gauntlet. Behind it a broad-shouldered sergeant with ink on her fingers works through the queue. She asks each traveller the same question, takes their coppers, scratches a line in a ledger and waves them on.

The cat walks the parapet beside you as if it owns the bridge. At the barrier post it stops and sniffs a chalk mark on the stone. The mark is fresh, not yet smudged by rain or boots, and it is Tymora's coin-sign, face up. Nobody in the queue looks at it.

Just past the barrier, under a hanging lantern, a gnome in a patched velvet coat shuffles a deck with practised fingers on an upturned crate. "One hand, friends, just one, Lady Luck's awake tonight!" The cards whisper as they fall.

The merchant ahead of you pays and steps through. The sergeant dips her pen, looks up and fixes you with a tired, measuring stare. "Next. Name, and what's your business in the Gate?"

screens:
The session begins.

Dusk settles over the Chionthar as you step onto Wyrm's Crossing. The bridge is less a bridge than a street hung over the water: shopfronts jammed shoulder to shoulder, washing strung between upper windows, hawkers selling hot eels and fried dough to anyone who slows down. Ahead, the Basilisk Gate rises dark against the last of the light, and before it a queue grinds forward past a Flaming Fist checkpoint. A broad-shouldered sergeant in a red-trimmed tabard is reading papers by lantern light, pulling a cart aside here, waving a family through there, and casting a long look at a pair of tiefling porters. Your cat walks close to your boots, tail high, ears turning at every shout. Then, off to one side, a voice cuts through the noise: "Three cards, friends, one queen — find the Lady and she pays double!" Under a lamp, a lean man in a patched green coat shuffles a deck on an upturned barrel, fingers quick and easy. Two dockhands are already playing. And at the empty side of the barrel, where a third player would sit, lies a single coin with Tymora's smiling face turned up — placed with care, untouched, as if the seat were reserved. The dealer catches your eye, and his smile widens. "You've the look of a man the Lady likes. Sit a hand?" Behind you, the queue to the gate shuffles forward a step. The lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge, and the city is waiting on the other side of the wall.

James stops a pace short of the barrel. Up close, Tobin Leck's smile is wider than his eyes. When James says *arrangement*, the dealer's hands go on shuffling, but the rhythm slips once, a card riffling a fraction late. The coin on the barrel's empty side looks old and silver, its edge soft with wear. The Lady's face on it is turned up to the lamp. The coin at James's throat has warmed a little more, like a hand pressed flat against his chest.

"Mine," Tobin says, too quickly. "Old piece, keeps the seat warm. I put her out every night face down, for luck, and if the Lady's minded she turns her —" He stops and laughs once, high and thin. "Figure of speech, friend. Figure of speech."

James has spent too many nights across tables from men like this to miss it. It's a lie, and a frightened one, not a clever one. The dealer's eyes keep going back to the coin as if it had moved while he wasn't looking. His left hand leaves the deck for a moment, presses flat against the breast of the green coat over something sewn or tucked inside, and then goes back to the cards. Whatever Tobin is, he isn't waiting for James with a knife. He looks like a man who has just been dealt a card he didn't want.

"Deal, Tobin," says the bigger of the two dockhands, Harl, tapping his stake on the wood. Bede, the younger one, looks from James to the silver coin and back. Then he edges his own coins a finger's width closer to himself.

Behind James the bridge goes on with its business. The queue shuffles another step toward the Basilisk Gate. A hawker shouts about eels. At the checkpoint the sergeant in the red-trimmed tabard looks up from her papers, takes in the man standing at the card-barrel without sitting, and goes back to her lantern. Nobody in the crowd is drifting closer. Nobody he can see, anyway.

The cat hasn't moved from his boot, but its ears have gone flat and its tail has wrapped tight around its paws. Through the pact bond comes a feeling with no words in it: *warm, old, hers* — the same smell as the coin at his own throat. Under that is something sour and newer, like a scratch on a clean thing.

Tobin squares the deck with a snap and puts on a good imitation of a grin. "Arrangement with the Lady," he says. "Don't hear that every night on the Crossing. What sort of arrangement does a man make with Tymora that keeps him off a deck, eh?"

James lets the breath out through his nose and looks at the river for a while. The Chionthar runs black under the bridge, carrying lamplight in pieces. Three men with coppers in their teeth.

When he turns back and says his piece, Tobin listens like a man being read his own sentence and finding it shorter than he feared. As the story goes on his mouth moves a little, repeating it: *soldier's cloak, Tethyrian patch, a cat, the Elfsong*. At *arrangement with the Lady* he flinches.

"She'll like that," he says. "The arrangement. She'll like that a lot, and I'll be honest, I don't like that she'll like it." He rubs his jaw. "But it's true, and I can say a true thing without my face doing anything. Yeah. Yeah, all right."

Then James asks his two questions, and Tobin answers fast. He's had them in his head for weeks with nobody to ask.

"Alone on the stairs. Always. She comes down from the top, not up from the water, and she stands two steps above me so I'm looking up at her. But there's a boat." He keeps his voice down even though nobody is near. "Every time. A little skiff under the first arch, tied off to the footing, lantern hooded. Man at the oars, or maybe more than one. I never see a face, just a shape and an oar resting. She never looks at it, and that's how I know it's hers." He swallows. "Water's right there, see. That's the bit I think about."

"Gloves stay on. Grey kid, buttoned at the wrist. She's never once touched my hand. The gold comes out of a little drawstring purse, and she tips it into my palm from above, the way you'd feed a dog you don't want licking you." His fingers twitch toward his side pocket, where the old silver coin is, and stop short. "And she always asks the same three things, same order. Where's he drinking. What did he win. Is he still winning." He looks at James and works it out. "You didn't win anything, friend. You didn't play. She'll ask, and I'll have to say *nothing*, and I don't know what she makes of a man the coin turns for who won't sit at a table."

While Tobin talks, James studies the Rock end of the bridge.

Wyrm's Rock rises out of the middle of the Crossing, a squat fortress sitting on an island of black stone, its walls lit by a few high windows. Where the street of shops meets the Rock's footing, about three hundred feet off, there's a gap between a rope-maker's and a shuttered eel stall. A single lamp on an iron arm hangs over it, and the top of a stone stair drops away under the lamp into the dark. James can't see the landing from here. The bridge's edge and the curve of the footing hide it. He can see what's above it, though. The rope-maker has a loft with a hoist-beam and a hatch half open. The roof of the eel stall is flat, tarred and low, with a stack of crates behind it. And under the bridge itself, where the first great arch springs from the Rock, there's a dark line along the stone that could be a ledge, or a drain, or nothing. Anyone who wanted to watch the stairs from above would pick the loft or the stall roof. Anyone who wanted to watch from the water would already be in a boat.

James sends his thought down the bond. The answer isn't a feeling of obedience, and it doesn't feel like fear either. It's lower and warmer than either: *yes*, with the sense of a body settling onto its haunches. Something under it has been waiting since the road to be let off the leash. The cat's tail unwraps from its paws and the tip of it starts, very slowly, to twitch.

At the gate, Sergeant Varn waves a cart of onions through without looking at it. She's looking past it, at the railing.

Tobin follows her glance, then pulls his coat tighter. "You're going in, then. Elfsong." He says it almost as a question, like a man checking his lines before he goes on. "And she's going to come looking for you there, because I told her to. That's — you know that's what you're doing, yeah? You're putting yourself on the barrel."

The room is about what two nights' money buys. There's a narrow bed with a bolster, a washstand with a chipped jug, a table and one chair, a lamp, a row of pegs, and a small rag rug that someone once cared about. The ceiling comes down at a slant over the bed, low enough that a tall man would learn about it in the night.

He goes to the window first. It's a casement with small leaded panes and a latch that sticks before it gives. Below is the yard he crossed coming in: cobbles, the worn lintel's lamp throwing a yellow fan over the door, and the mouth of the hops-smelling lane at the far side. It's a long drop to the cobbles, fifteen feet or a bit more, onto stone. A little to the left and about six feet down, though, is the mossy slate roof of a woodshed built against the wall. A man could let himself down onto that from the sill without a rope, and onto a water butt at the corner from there. Nobody is in the yard. A cart stands empty by the brewery wall with its shafts on the ground.

Then he lays out the room the way a careless man would. He opens the pack on the bed and leaves the bedroll half out. The crossbow and the quiver of bolts lean in the corner where the door would show them to anyone who looked in. He spreads the pay slip flat on the table under the lamp, *James Worgen* face up in a regimental clerk's tidy hand. The promissory note and the deck go back inside his jacket, against his ribs. The rod, the cloak, the coin on its cord and the two red potions stay where they are.

He sits on the bed with his back to the wall, under the slope of the ceiling, and reaches down the bond.

For a while there's nothing, only the far, cottony silence of a link stretched past where it can carry. The common room's noise comes up through the floorboards: a laugh, a chair scraping. Somewhere along the passage a door opens and closes. Then, a little before the three-quarter hour, the bond catches like a fish taking a line.

What comes first is a jumble of road, the way it always comes when the cat is moving fast: cobbles, a gutter, the hops wall, and below all of it the cat's pleasure at being out and running with a job to do. Then the memory, pushed at him whole, the way a cat brings you something it's caught. There's lantern heat on its back and boot leather under it, a worn boot that smells of horse and the bridge, and a woman's voice just above. The voice isn't speaking to him. It's counting under its breath along with the tail on the stone, one, two, up to six, and then a seventh beat where the tail stops and nothing comes.

*"Six,"* in that flat checkpoint voice. Then the boot shifts under it, slowly, the way you move a foot when something is sitting on it that you've decided not to kick.

So Varn has her six.

Behind that comes the bridge, seen from the gate at cat height, all legs and wheels and lamplight in a long line. There's Tobin's barrel and its lamp, still lit. Tobin is under it and shuffling, and the smell coming off him is sharper than it was at dusk, like sweat gone cold. Past him, three hundred feet down the Crossing toward the black hump of the Rock, the cat shows him something it noticed because it was different. At dusk a lamp on an iron arm hung over the gap by the rope-maker's. Now there's only the arm. The gap is dark, a missing tooth in the row of lit shopfronts, and the head of the stair is somewhere inside it.

The cat doesn't know what that means, and doesn't pretend to. It only knows the place has changed, so it brings it to him.

Then the common room arrives through its eyes, warm and close: the door, the dwarves' boots, the hearthstone. In the corner, the velvet collar sits straight-backed, both hands on the wood, with no dice in them. The cat turns twice on the warm stone and lies down facing the corner. The bond settles into something low and steady. *Here. Watching.*

James stands, faces the dark window glass and lets the Lady's mask come over him.

It takes a few muttered words and a pass of the hand down the face. Nobody would remember it as anything if they saw it. In the glass, a different man looks back at him. He's a Rivington boatman, broader in the face and older, with grey through a short beard and a nose that has been out in a lot of weather. The Tethyrian cloak is gone. In its place is a dockhand's canvas jacket, tar-stained at the cuffs, with the collar turned up and a knitted cap pulled down. His boots look like boots that have stood in bilge water. The coin on its cord has vanished under a collar that isn't there. Beneath it all, the cloak still hangs from his shoulders, light and real, and the old enchantment in it sits close and quiet as ever.

Below him the common room goes on, loud and yellow. The way down is the stair he came up. It ends at the foot of the room, in full view of the bar and of Hesper, who wrote *James Worgen* in her book an hour ago and has watched everyone who has gone up those stairs tonight. The other way is the window, the woodshed and the yard.

It's about ten to ten.

James breathes the words down through the boards: *if your da ever asks, I was a sack.*

Below him there's a snort, and the rustle of a blanket. "Sacks don't pay," Dace says. That's all she says.

He moves along the tar on his belly, one hand and then one knee, spreading his weight the way you cross a frozen pond. Nothing rocks this time. The roof gives a little under him and stays quiet. At the back left corner the drainpipe comes up out of the dark, cold and furred with old rust. He gets his cheek against the edge of the roof beside it and looks down.

The parapet falls away under him, and below it the Rock's footing. It's black stone, sheer, wet for the last few feet above the water. The ring is about twenty-five feet down and a little to his left, set into the stone just where the first great arch springs from the footing. It's iron, as big as a man's spread hand, and in what little light comes off the water it shows as a darker circle on dark stone. A frayed tail of old rope hangs from it, too short to be any use to anyone.

The current comes out from under the arch on his right and slides away to his left toward the harbour, smooth and fast, with little dimples on top where it curls round the footing. Anything tied to that ring would swing downstream and lie along the stone, out of the arch's mouth and in its shadow.

The dark line he saw at dusk is a ledge. It's a stone walk no wider than a boot is long, a foot above the water, slick with weed. It runs along the footing from the ring toward the bridge for about twenty feet, to where the last few steps of the stair come down out of the gap. Those he can just see, three or four treads shining wet, and then a small square landing at the water's edge. From a boat at the ring you could step onto the ledge, sidle along it with a hand on the wall, and come out at the bottom of the stair. From the top of the stair you could come down and never know a boat was there unless you looked along the footing. *She never looks at it,* Tobin said.

James fixes it in his eye. Then he settles in. His cap is down and his cheek is on the warm tar. One eye watches the stair head through the gap, the other the black under the arch, and he breathes the slow breath of a picket.

Down the bond he sends a light touch: *Where are you? Is the collar home yet?*

Nothing comes back. There's only the cottony nothing of a link stretched past where it reaches, like calling down a well with no water in it. Wherever the cat is, it's still in the Lower City, a long way off over the wall.

The bridge empties around him. A last cart goes by toward Rivington with its axle squealing. Two men pass the gap talking about a horse, and don't look at it. Back up the Crossing Tobin's patter goes on under his lamp, *find the Lady, find the Lady*, with longer gaps in it now. Nobody is there to hear it. The tar cools under James's chest. The river talks to the stones.

At a quarter to eleven he feels the edges of the face start to thin, like a coat going threadbare at the elbows. He puts a hand up and drags it down his jaw the way a man rubs himself awake, and mutters the words into his collar. The grey beard and the weathered nose settle back over him as before. To anyone counting, nothing has changed.

From under the boards, very low, comes Dace's voice: "Whatever that was, do it quieter."

The eleventh bell sounds from somewhere up the hill, then another, a beat behind, from farther off. Under the arch the black stays black.

A little before half past, the bond catches.

The first thing he gets is speed: cobbles, the Basilisk Gate's cold echo, bridge planks. Then the cat pushes the memory at him whole. A lantern bigger than the boy carrying it bobs along a street of narrow houses below the Counting House, and two pairs of legs walk in its light: small quick boots, and good shoes in no hurry. Nobody walks behind them. The cat checked more than once, from a wall-top and a doorway. The good shoes stop at a green door, and the door closes behind them. A minute later a candle comes into a window at the far end of the house, high up, burns for about as long as it takes to turn a key, and goes out. A candle lights in a different window, then that one goes out too.

*Home,* the cat says, in its way. *Both.*

Then it's on the crates behind him. It climbs them without rocking a single one, and he gets the faint feeling it intends him to notice that. It flows onto the roof and lies down against his hip, its ears pointed at the water.

Time goes slowly the way it does on a picket, a few breaths at a time. The cold comes up out of the river into the stone. Tobin's patter stops for a while, then starts again. It's getting on for twenty to midnight when the cat's ears go flat and then forward, both at once, toward the left. That's downstream, out past the end of the footing where the river opens toward the harbour.

James listens for what it heard.

The cat finds him with its nose before anything else.

It can't see much down the stair. Its eyes give James three wet treads, the square of the landing and black water, with the slit of orange from the hooded lantern far along the footing. The smell is what comes clear, and the cat sorts it the way it would sort a mousehole. On the boat there's wet wool, tar and a big man's sweat, the one at the oars, who hasn't moved. Then there's a second man, closer, much closer. He's standing on the stone beside the bottom step with his back to the wall of the footing, six feet below the cat's chin, so still that his eyes would never have found him. He smells of oiled leather and old iron, and under both is the same thin sweetness the cat didn't like on the water. It's stronger on him, as if it were in his clothes. The bundle in the bottom of the boat smells of new rope and something heavy and cold, like a bag of stones.

Then the count comes, the cat's way: one there, one there, and nothing else alive under the arch. *Two.* There's a pause, and then it adds what it thinks of the near one: *waiting, like me.*

James keeps his own eyes on the bridge.

Tobin comes first. James hears him before he sees him. The barrel goes over onto its side with a hollow knock somewhere up toward the gate, a lamp handle clinks, and then there are footsteps, quick and uneven, a man trying to walk at an ordinary pace. The green coat passes along the row of shuttered fronts, darker than the dark between the lamps. At the gap he stops. Through the bond James feels the cat go flat as a shadow on its step, and he feels Tobin see it. The dealer's smell jumps, sharp and sour. He stands at the top of the stair for two breaths that last too long, looking down at a cat on a step at midnight. He doesn't say anything. Then he steps over it, carefully, the way you step over a sleeping dog, and goes down. The cat's nose follows him to the landing, where he stops two steps from the bottom. That puts him within an arm's reach of the man against the wall, and he doesn't know it.

The cat's next thought has no words in it. It's a feeling of *wrong*, aimed at the near man. He has turned his head toward Tobin, slowly.

Then James sees her.

She comes from the Rivington end, from the south, the far side of the Rock from the gate, along the length of the Crossing he has had in view all night. The first he sees of her is a pale shape passing under the last lit lamp, two hundred feet off. Her grey cloak catches the light and gives it back like dust. She walks unhurried and straight-backed, down the middle of the planking. She doesn't stay in the shadow of the fronts. She looks like a woman who has every right to be on a bridge at midnight and expects anyone who meets her to step aside. Her hood is up and her gloved hands are folded in front of her. She doesn't look back once.

James watches the bridge behind her as far as the lamps reach. He sees nobody. No second shape comes under the lamp after her, and nobody is idling in a doorway. The planking behind her is empty all the way back to the dark beyond the last light. If anyone is following her at a hundred feet, he's doing it somewhere James can't see.

She comes along the fronts and passes beneath the eel stall's roof, so close he could drop his cap on her hood. He smells something faint and clean on the air after her, like cold ash. At the gap she stops at the head of the stair, under the iron arm with its dead lamp.

She stands there, looking down.

Through the bond James feels the cat's whole body go tight on the cold step, and then he feels it do as it was told. One forepaw comes up and a rough tongue goes over it, slowly, like a cat with nothing on its mind but its own fur.

The woman in grey doesn't go down yet. James hears her voice for the first time, from right below his roof. It's soft and warm, pitched the way you'd speak to a child half asleep.

"Well," she says. "And who are *you*?"

The midnight bell hasn't rung yet.

[Onward]

The cat comes up off the cold step all at once, the way a cat stands when it has decided to be bored. It puts its front legs out, then its back legs, and gives one long, rusty *mrrp* up at the grey hood, as if anyone standing on a stair at midnight must have fish on them. Then it walks straight past her, close enough that its tail brushes her hem.

Through the bond James gets what the cat got at her ankle. Cold ash first. Under the ash, and so strong it makes the cat's whiskers flatten, is the Lady's smell. It's the warm old smell of the coin at his throat and Tobin's coin on the barrel, but there's a lot of it, as if she has a purse full. Every trace of it carries the same sour scratch the cat caught on the barrel at dusk.

A grey glove comes down. One kid-covered fingertip runs along the cat's spine, from the shoulders to the root of the tail, light as a dressmaker measuring. Then it's gone.

"Go on, then," she says to it, warm and amused. "There's nothing for you on me."

The cat goes three paces up the bridge, sits with its back to her and starts washing a shoulder, unhurried.

Above her, James moves. He gets his left hand under the canvas jacket and closes it on the rod, then slides back the last foot along the tar to the drainpipe corner. He spreads his weight and lets the roof take it slowly. The tar doesn't creak, and nothing knocks. Under him, Dace's breathing doesn't change. Under the dead lamp, the woman in grey doesn't look up. He gets his cheek back against the roof's edge beside the cold pipe, with the ring, the ledge and the wet bottom treads in his eye, all in silence.

He hears her go down. Her soft shoes make a small sound on each wet step, at an even pace, never hurrying. After a while her cloak comes into his sight below. He can see it against the black because it catches the little orange from the hooded lantern and holds it like dust. She stops on the stair, two steps above a darker shape that must be Tobin. Tobin's breathing carries all the way up to the roof.

The cat finishes its shoulder, gets up and pours itself into the gap to Pell's step. It lies flat with its nose over the edge. *Landing. Him. Still.*

Somewhere up the hill the midnight bell starts. A second one answers it, farther off.

The woman waits until both have finished.

"Did it turn?"

"It turned." Tobin's voice comes up thin but steady. "Fastest I ever saw it, lady. Before he was off the road."

"Where's he drinking?"

That's the first question, in the same order Tobin said she always uses.

"Elfsong. I sent him. Asked me where he'd get a bed and not be robbed, and I said the Elfsong."

"What did he win?"

"Nothing." He says it plainly, the way James gave it to him. "He didn't play, so he didn't win. Wouldn't sit. Wouldn't touch the deck."

Nothing comes from the stair for a long moment, only the river and the *plip* off the shipped oars.

She doesn't ask the third question.

"Tell me what he said." Her voice is gentler than before. "All of it. Slowly."

Tobin tells her. It comes out the way James built it: a soldier's cloak, a Tethyrian patch, came in alone, wouldn't sit. When he gets to *an arrangement with the Lady*, James hears her let out a breath. It's soft and pleased, almost a laugh, the sound of someone opening a present.

"And a cat," Tobin says. "He had a cat with him."

The pleased sound stops.

"A cat." She lets it rest there. "What sort of cat?"

"Just—" Tobin's voice catches. "Just a cat, lady. Ordinary. Walks at his boots."

The cat on Pell's step feels his eyes before James can see anything. A man's look comes up the stair from the bottom and lands on it, a frightened look that stays a heartbeat too long. Then the grey hood turns, slowly, and lifts toward the gap at the top of the stair, where a cat lies with its nose over the edge.

"Well," she says, very softly.

She doesn't move. She speaks past Tobin, to the dark beside the bottom step, the way you'd ask a servant to see to the fire.

"Bring me the cat. Gently. I don't want it hurt."

The bond jolts. *Moves.* A creak of oiled leather comes off the wet wall, and a hand comes away from the stone. Below James, a shape darker than the footing peels off the wall and steps onto the shining bottom tread, close enough to Tobin to brush him. For the first time all night James's own eyes can find it: broad, hooded, starting up the stair without a sound. About thirty feet of steps lie between it and the cat on Pell's step.

Tobin hasn't moved at all.

The order goes down the bond like a kick, and the cat takes it the way a cat takes a door slammed behind it.

It comes up off Pell's step in one movement, ears back and belly low. The hooded man is still ten treads from the top. For half a heartbeat James sees him through the cat's eyes from above: a broad shoulder, a hand coming up, open, the fingers spread the way you hold them out to a dog you mean to grab. Then the cat is gone. It doesn't run down the bridge toward the eel stall. It runs up, toward the gate, a grey streak along the shuttered fronts.

James lies still. His cheek is on the tar and his fist is closed around the rod under the canvas.

The cat makes it, but only just. The hooded man reaches the top of the stair in time to see it go under the first lit lamp, flat out and low to the planking. Past the lamp is a stretch of dark between two lights, with the carter's empty wagon standing in it, the shafts down. The cat goes under the wagon and doesn't come out the side he's watching. Through the bond James gets wheel-spokes, axle grease, cold cobbles, a shutter with a broken slat, then the gate passage's echo, all in a rush. Then comes the smell of horse and wet stone, a lantern's heat overhead, and a pair of worn boots that know it. Varn is still under the arch, passing the lantern to a night man James doesn't know. A boot shifts and then goes still with the cat pressed against its heel, its heart going like a drum. Above it the flat voice says, very quietly, "Again."

At the stair head the hooded man stands in the gap a yard from James's cap and looks up the bridge for a long time.

James can hear him breathe through his nose, slow and steady, and smell him: oiled leather, old iron, and under them the thin sweetness the cat didn't like, close enough now to taste. The man looks up the Crossing to the lamps, and then along the shuttered fronts on either side. His hood turns toward the eel stall and passes over it at the height of the shutters. It never lifts to the roof. He doesn't see the man lying on the tar above him, or the grey beard, or the fist inside the canvas jacket. As far as he can tell, the bridge is empty planking and a cat that's gone.

He goes back down without a sound.

James keeps the bottom treads in his eye. The grey cloak hasn't moved off its step. The hooded shape stops below her and shakes its head once. It doesn't say a word.

"No matter." Her voice comes up warm and unhurried, as if the cat had been a hope and not a need. "Cats come back to where they're fed."

Then she turns to Tobin. He's been standing so still that James had almost lost him against the stone.

"You looked at it, Tobin." She's gentle about it. "When you said *cat*. You looked straight up the stairs at it, like a little boy who's been told not to look at the cake." She waits. Tobin doesn't answer. "We don't look at things. Do we."

"No, lady." It comes out cracked.

A grey glove moves. James sees the purse come out on its drawstring, and he hears it before he sees anything else: one coin and then a second, falling from above into an open palm. It's gold, not rope.

"Two," she says. "One for him. One for being a good boy next time." The purse goes away. "Put it out tomorrow night, the same as always. If he comes back past your barrel, you'll tell me how he walks and who he's with. If he doesn't come back, you'll tell me that too."

She doesn't wait for him to say yes. She comes up the stair as she went down it, never hurrying. Her cloak catches the last of the hooded lantern's orange and loses it again. She passes under the eel stall roof close enough that James could drop his cap on her hood. He smells the cold ash again, and then she's out on the planking. She turns south toward the Rivington end, the way she came, and walks down the middle of the bridge with her gloved hands folded in front of her.

Under the arch, the hooded man edges back along the ledge with one hand on the wall. Rope scrapes through iron. A blade slips into the water, wrapped and silent, and the skiff moves off the footing. It drifts more than it rows, sliding away downstream on the current toward the harbour, hooded lantern and bag of stones and all. Within a few breaths it's only a darker patch on dark water, and then James can't tell it from the river.

Tobin is still on the landing. He's two steps from the bottom with his fist closed around two gold pieces, and he hasn't moved since she left.

From under the boards, so low it's almost nothing, comes Dace's voice: "She gone?"

The grey cloak is a pale smudge under the lamps toward Rivington, a hundred feet off and getting further. Down the bond the cat's heartbeat is slowing against Varn's boot, three hundred feet up the bridge the other way. It's a few minutes past midnight, and the boatman's face will hold until about a quarter to one.

James doesn't look back at the stair. Tobin is somewhere below in the dark, two steps from the bottom with gold in his fist and no rope round his neck, and James leaves him there. She is a pale smudge under the lamps toward Rivington, walking down the middle of the bridge.

[Onward]

She is easy to keep in sight and hard to follow without being seen.

After midnight the Crossing is a long, bare street of planking between the shuttered fronts. Every third lamp still burns, and most of the doorways are dark. There's nobody to walk behind. James does it the only way an empty street allows: he doesn't follow her, he walks home along the same road. He keeps to the opposite side of the bridge, about a hundred feet back, and never passes under a lamp while she's under one. When she's in the light, he's in the dark between two lamps. When she steps out of it, he lets his own lamp take him for a few strides, cap down, a tired man in tarry canvas. The boots put him down on the old boards without a sound. Without them his heels would be the only noise on the whole bridge.

Halfway past the Rock she stops.

She doesn't turn her head. She stands at the rail with her gloved hands on it and looks downstream, toward the harbour, where the skiff went. She waits for as long as it takes to say a short prayer. James is between two lamps when she stops, and he stops too. He turns to the parapet, leans his forearms on it and spits into the river, the way men do on bridges at night. When she moves on, he gives her ten heartbeats and then moves on himself.

She never looks back. Twice, though, she slows under a lamp, the way you slow when you're listening behind you, and walks on when she hears nothing. James lets the gap open to a hundred and twenty feet and keeps it there.

The Rivington end of the bridge widens out into a cobbled square where the road comes down off the planking. There's a horse trough, a shuttered toll-house, and one lantern on a post by the trough. A man is sitting on the trough's edge with his elbows on his knees.

He stands up when she comes off the bridge. He's young and lanky, in a sailor's short coat with a scarf wound twice round his throat. She doesn't stop walking. He falls in beside her for six or seven strides, his head bent toward her hood, and James is too far off to hear a word of it. He sees her hand come out of the folded pair, palm down and level, the way you show a child how tall someone is. She moves it a little, once. The young man nods, and nods again. Then he turns back and walks onto the Crossing toward the city, whistling under his breath, his hands in his pockets.

That road runs right past James.

James is at the rail on the bridge's last stretch, cap down, doing what boatmen do with a river at night. The whistling comes up the planking. It's a sea tune, half the notes wrong. The young man passes at arm's length. Up close he's maybe twenty, with a long jaw, a chipped front tooth and the scarf pulled up to his chin. His eyes touch the Rivington boatman at the rail and slide off him, as they would off a post. Then he's gone north under the lamps, toward the Rock and the Basilisk Gate and the Lower City beyond it, at the pace of a man with an errand and no hurry about it.

James straightens up. The grey cloak is crossing the square.

She doesn't take the river road. She goes uphill, into the lanes of Rivington behind the waterfront, where the houses are wood on stone footings and lean together over streets too narrow for a cart. These streets are easier for him than the bridge was. They're crooked, half of them unlit, and they smell of tanning, wet ash and somebody's late supper. He loses her twice at corners and finds her again by the pale cloak at the far end of the next lane, both times. There's no one else on these streets except a dog that comes to a gate, looks at her, and lies back down without making a sound.

At a short, steep lane with a cooper's yard at the bottom, where hoops are stacked against a wall, she stops at a door.

It's a narrow house, three storeys, the ground floor stone and the upper two wood, with dark shutters on every window. It's plainer than its neighbours and better kept. James stops at the corner by the cooper's yard, in the black under the eaves. From sixty feet away he watches her hand go into her cloak and come out with a key. The glove stays on. The door opens inward onto darkness, she steps through, and it closes. He hears no bolt. Either it makes no sound or she didn't draw one.

A few breaths later a thin line of light shows between the shutters on the second floor. It stays there for about the time it takes to take off a cloak and gloves and lay them down. Then it goes out.

No one else comes up the lane, or out of the house. The cooper's yard is dark. Somewhere down the hill a ship's bell sounds the half hour across the water.

There's something nailed over the door, in the lintel, and in the starlight it took him a while to make out what it was. Now he's sure. It's a horseshoe, old and rust-dark, hung with its points down.

James has known what that means since he was nine. Every carter, every sailor and every man who ever sat at a gaming table knows it. Points up, the shoe holds the luck in, like a cup. Points down, it pours the luck out onto whoever walks under it. Nobody hangs a shoe that way by accident. When people do it, they're doing it to someone's door, as a curse. It's rare for anyone to do it to their own.

At the edge of his reach the bond flickers and catches, faint and thin. He gets lantern heat, the river, and stone steps going down to water, the Rivington steps somewhere below the bridge. The worn boots are walking fast, and a waterman's voice is grumbling about the hour. The cat is at the sergeant's heel, as it was told. A moment later the steps drop out of range and the bond goes quiet again.

The lane is empty. The boatman's face is good until about a quarter to one.

I stop a pace short of the barrel and don't sit. My hand goes to the cord at my neck without my meaning it to — the coin there is warm, as it always is now. I look at the twin of it lying in the empty seat, then at the dealer.

"The Lady and I have an arrangement," I say, easy, keeping my hands where he can see them and well away from the cards. "Part of it is that I don't touch a deck. So I'll stand, if it's all the same." I nod at the coin on the barrel. "Who left that there? You, or someone who was expecting me?"

I keep an eye on the two dockhands and the bridge behind me while he answers — a man who knows my face before I've shown it to the city is either a priest or a problem. The cat sits down against my boot, watching the dealer's hands.

I let the question sit while Tobin deals Harl his three cards, and I watch the deal — not to play, just old habit, the way you watch a man's hands when he's nervous. Then I step round to his side of the barrel, close enough that the dockhands won't catch every word, and drop my voice.

"The sort where I lost everything once and she gave it back on her terms. Keeping the deck out of my hands is the cheap part." I nod down at the silver coin without touching it. "That one's hers too. I can feel it from here, and so can you, or you wouldn't have told me a lie that bad. You're not a priest, Tobin, and you don't look like a thief who's happy with his take." I glance, once, at the breast of his coat where his hand went. "So here's how I'd rather this goes. Finish your hand with these two, then you and I walk ten paces down the bridge where the Fist can see us but can't hear us, and you tell me where you got it and what's riding in your coat. I'm not the Watch, and I'm not here to take anything off you. I'm the man the seat was kept for — you said as much yourself."

I keep my tone friendly and tired, like a sergeant giving a frightened recruit the easy way out, and I let him see I mean it. The cat stays where it is, watching the coin.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I let out a breath through my nose and look out at the water for a moment before I answer. Three men with coppers in their teeth. Paid to the sea.

"You tell her the truth, Tobin. All of it that she'd learn anyway." I turn back to him. "A man came in off the Way at dusk, alone, soldier's cloak, Tethyrian patch, with a cat. Coin turned the moment he set foot on the bridge, fastest you've ever seen. He wouldn't sit, said he had an arrangement with the Lady, and asked where he could find a bed and a drink in the Lower City. You sent him to the Elfsong. That's where he'll be." I tap the rail. "That's all true, so you won't have to act it. Lie to a woman like that and she'll smell it, and then it's your name next on that lining — I'd rather she keeps thinking you're a gold-a-head fool who writes nothing down."

I keep my voice low and even. "Two things, quick, before I go through the gate. Does she come alone to the stairs, or does she have someone standing off? And how does she pay you — coin from her own hand, or does she keep her gloves on?"

While he answers, I'm already looking at the Rock end of the bridge — where the stairs would be, what overlooks them, where a man could sit in the dark and watch a meeting without being part of it. The cat gets a thought down the bond: *tonight you go first, and you go quiet.*

"I know what I'm doing. I've been bait before — in Tethyr we called it a picket." I give him a half-smile that doesn't reach anything. "Somebody's paying the sea with men the Lady smiled on. I'm her envoy, and I came here to find out how I serve. I think I just did."

I push off the rail. "About the winning. Say it plain — he didn't play, so he didn't win. That's the truth and it'll trouble her more than any lie would. Let her chew on it." I glance at the lining of his coat. "And Tobin — after tonight, that coat goes in a chest and you buy a new one. Keep the gold she gives you in a separate purse and don't spend it; you may need to show somebody where it came from one day. If anything goes wrong on those stairs, don't run along the bridge. Run *up*, toward the gate and the lanterns. She's got a boat; she hasn't got the Fist."

I don't tell him I'll be watching. A frightened man looks where he knows a friend is sitting, and I want his eyes on her and nowhere else.

"Go deal another hour. Act like a man who just had a dull conversation with a tired soldier." I nod toward the gate. "Elfsong, then. If I'm ever in the seat, I'll say Tobin sent me."

I walk back into the queue and let Sergeant Varn get a good look at my papers — the Tethyrian pay slip, my own face, the cat at my heel — a man coming into the city alone and above-board, exactly as the story goes. Once I'm through the Basilisk Gate, my plan is simple: find the Elfsong, take a room under my own name, leave the pack and the crossbow there where a curious eye can find them, eat something — and well before midnight come back out to the Crossing wearing a different face, to sit on the roof of that eel stall with a cat on the crates behind me and a view of the stairs.

I take the pay slip back and tuck it inside the cloak where it lives.

"He wanted me to sit a hand. I don't play — the Lady and I have an understanding on that score, and I keep it." I say it plain, soldier to soldier. "He wasn't used to hearing no, so he asked why, and I told him. Then I asked him where a man gets a bed and a meal in the Lower City without being robbed in his sleep, and he said the Elfsong. That's the whole of it." A tired shrug. "Business is finding out what my business is. I came off a long road with a purse I'd rather not carry round the Outer City after dark, and that cat has opinions about where we sleep."

I let that sit, then lower my voice a notch, the way you do when you're asking a sergeant something off the roster. "You watched that barrel close for a man who wasn't cheating anyone tonight. Is Leck trouble, or is it the company he keeps?" I hold her eye and keep my hands easy. "I was a scout a long time, Sergeant. I don't ask that to make conversation. If there's something on this bridge the Fist is short of men to look at, I'd rather know whose lantern to run toward."

Then I step aside so the tiefling woman and her children can come up to the light, and wait on her answer.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I look at the open hand, then at the private's back, and I let the easy soldier's voice go. What's left is quieter.

The cat will come to your lantern — it knows your face now — and it'll sit a count of taps on the stone with its tail. Whatever it taps, that's my door. Nobody on the bridge looks twice at a cat."

I settle the pack on my shoulder. "Hire your waterman, Sergeant, and sit well out. If that skiff has to row past you, let it. I only want to know where it sleeps." And then I'm through the Basilisk Gate with the cat at my heel, into the Lower City, heading downhill toward the harbour and asking the first lamplighter I pass for the way to the Elfsong.

I eat, because a soldier eats when there's food, and I watch the dice table over the rim of the dwarves' brown.

The window, then. Hesper has seen one man go up those stairs tonight and I'd rather she only ever sees that one come down.

Then come to the Crossing — the flat roof of the eel stall by the dark gap, I'll be on it. If you can't find me there, go to the woman's boot at the gate and stay with her.*

I turn the lamp down low — not out — leave the pay slip under it, and work the casement latch. Over the sill, down onto the woodshed slates, the water butt, the cobbles. I cross the yard like a man who's just been round the back to piss, and take the hops lane out.

I don't go to the Rock end first. Flat on the tar, cap down, with the stair-head and the first arch below me and most of two hours to lie still in. I've lain in worse.
