**Player's note — James Worgen, session one**

**What worked**

The opening. I came in with no errand and inside two minutes I had one, and it grew out of my own character rather than being handed to me: the seat kept for me at the barrel was a hook I'd have bitten even if I hadn't been told to. By the end of the night I'd found a murder ring that pays the sea in Tymora's favourites, a frightened accomplice, a sergeant with four closed reports and a grudge, a boy on day ten of a Beshaba coin, a house in Rivington with a shoe hung points-down over its own door — and not one of those was a quest-giver. They were people with their own business who I happened to walk into. That's exactly the campaign the canon file promised.

The NPCs had voices I can still hear. Tobin's "I can do up." Varn's "Four." Hesper putting a tankard away upside down. Dace through the boards — "Sacks don't pay." Nobody was a clown, nobody was a signpost. Varn in particular: the GM let my Deception *fail* and then let the failure be the thing that got me what I wanted, because dropping the lie was the better play. That's good adjudication.

The cat. Best companion I've had at an AI table. It never spoke, never broke character, and the GM used the pact bond for sensory information (smells, "two", "wrong", "both — don't forget the other one") instead of exposition. The 100-foot telepathy limit was enforced and I didn't resent it, because the cat kept doing the sensible thing off-screen. The GM also made me *pay* for sending it — Tobin's glance up the stairs nearly cost me the whole picket. Fair.

Information economy. I was told exactly what a 19 Perception buys and what an 11 doesn't. I missed the skiff coming in and the GM didn't soften it; I got the boat already tied up and no count of the men in it. The world stayed honest to the dice.

Pacing of the picket. Two hours flat on a roof could have been dead air; it was tense the whole way, because small things kept arriving — the lamp, Dace, the eleventh bell, the cat's memory of the green door.

**What broke**

The roll cards. Three Persuasion/Deception cards showed "+2" while naming "Persuasion +7" as the source. The GM caught it and corrected in narration each time, but it meant I was reading two numbers and trusting the out-of-game note over the card. That's a server-side problem and it needs fixing before it lands on a roll where five points decide a life.

The reroll system. I asked to reroll the failed Stealth; the app rerolled the *successful* Perception on the card above it, turned a 19 into a 3, and left the 11 standing. The GM made it right — restored the 19, didn't charge the reroll — but the fix took three exchanges and a request for the correct narration. When two cards are stacked, the player needs to be able to point at which one. Also: a stale card (the Varn Deception from an hour earlier) resurfaced mid-roof and the GM had to guess what it was.

Duplicate narration. Several turns had the same beat told twice — once in prose, then again under a second "Out of game" heading as "told once more, as it happened." Once was enough. It read like the app re-sending a corrected message and the GM dutifully narrating both.

The log. The Dace check was recorded as "11 vs 15 — failure" after the proper reroll had made it a natural 20. The GM said it's corrected; I'd like to see that reflected in the records, not just promised.

Small thing: "Day 2 · night" ticked over at midnight, which is correct but jarred — I'd rather the day roll over at dawn or a long rest.

**What was missing**

No combat, so I can't speak to the fight rules, the numbers-in-the-note, or how the cat behaves under initiative. Deliberate on my part — I kept the rod sheathed — but it's untested.

Coin. I'm carrying 350 *gold* and nothing smaller, so I tipped a thirteen-year-old a gold piece and had to be waved off from overpaying an innkeeper. A soldier would have silver and copper in his purse. Could the sheet break the 350 into mixed coin, or could the GM let me change money at the first opportunity?

Clock pressure. The one thing that never bit was time. Varn's midnight bell, Hob at eleven, the disguise's hour — all were tracked and all were fine, but nothing I did was ever *too late*. That's probably right for a first night. I'd like to feel it next session, with Teo at midday and a skiff somewhere in the harbour that Varn may or may not have followed.

Tymora herself. The coin at my throat went warm and gave one cold prickle. That's the right amount for now, but she owes me a word eventually, and I'd like it to come when I least want it — ideally with a deck in front of me.

**Would I sit down again?** Tomorrow, at midday, at the Elfsong. Fix the cards first.

Yes. Three, and they're different kinds of "didn't."

**The one I'm still thinking about: the young man in the scarf.** When he came off the trough, took her instructions, and walked back up the bridge past me whistling — I had a choice I didn't get to make properly. He was heading north, toward the Basilisk Gate, toward the Lower City, almost certainly toward the Elfsong and a room with my name on the table. I wanted to let the grey cloak go and turn round after *him*. He's the errand; she's the house. The house will still be there tomorrow and the errand won't. I went after her because that was the plan I'd made on the roof, and because the picket had already cost me two rerolls and I didn't trust my luck to change course mid-stride. I think I chose wrong. I'd rather have a face and a door for the man who does the work than for the woman who gives the orders, because he's the one who'll be waiting in the dark on Steephill. If next session opens with something in room six that shouldn't be, that's on me.

**The one I'm sure I chose right but hated: the stairs.** When she said "bring me the cat" and the hooded man's hand came off the wall, I had the rod in my fist and a clear line down thirty feet of wet steps. Every instinct from Tethyr said *fire first*. I didn't, because a beam of light off a roof blows the picket, Varn's boat, Tobin's cover and probably Tobin's life, all for a cat that can run. It was right. It still felt like leaving a man behind. The GM made the cat's escape a 13 against 13 — I felt every point of that.

**The one I didn't want to want: Teo's dice.** "One more, Corrie, I *can't* lose." The dice were right there on the wood and I'd just spent an hour watching his hand go to his pocket. For a breath I wanted to pick them up and show him — show *myself* — that the streak was the coin and not the boy. The GM never pushed; the file says the DM may tempt him and this time the table was tempting enough on its own. I'd like it pushed harder next time. A ban nobody tests isn't a ban.

And one smaller thing that's about the app, not the character: after the reroll misfired, I didn't ask for a third card operation I'd otherwise have wanted — on the skiff Perception, where an 11 cost me the headcount in the boat. I'd spent both rerolls and had Inspiration left, and I kept it for steel partly because the machinery had just burned me and I didn't want another three-exchange repair at the tensest moment of the night. That's a cost of the broken cards you won't see in the log.

I stop a pace short of the barrel and don't sit. My hand goes to the cord at my neck without my meaning it to — the coin there is warm, as it always is now. I look at the twin of it lying in the empty seat, then at the dealer.

"The Lady and I have an arrangement," I say, easy, keeping my hands where he can see them and well away from the cards. "Part of it is that I don't touch a deck. So I'll stand, if it's all the same." I nod at the coin on the barrel. "Who left that there? You, or someone who was expecting me?"

turns.reply:
James stops a pace short of the barrel. Up close, Tobin Leck's smile is wider than his eyes. When James says *arrangement*, the dealer's hands go on shuffling, but the rhythm slips once, a card riffling a fraction late. The coin on the barrel's empty side looks old and silver, its edge soft with wear. The Lady's face on it is turned up to the lamp. The coin at James's throat has warmed a little more, like a hand pressed flat against his chest.

"Mine," Tobin says, too quickly. "Old piece, keeps the seat warm. I put her out every night face down, for luck, and if the Lady's minded she turns her —" He stops and laughs once, high and thin. "Figure of speech, friend. Figure of speech."

James has spent too many nights across tables from men like this to miss it. It's a lie, and a frightened one, not a clever one. The dealer's eyes keep going back to the coin as if it had moved while he wasn't looking. His left hand leaves the deck for a moment, presses flat against the breast of the green coat over something sewn or tucked inside, and then goes back to the cards. Whatever Tobin is, he isn't waiting for James with a knife. He looks like a man who has just been dealt a card he didn't want.

"Deal, Tobin," says the bigger of the two dockhands, Harl, tapping his stake on the wood. Bede, the younger one, looks from James to the silver coin and back. Then he edges his own coins a finger's width closer to himself.

Behind James the bridge goes on with its business. The queue shuffles another step toward the Basilisk Gate. A hawker shouts about eels. At the checkpoint the sergeant in the red-trimmed tabard looks up from her papers, takes in the man standing at the card-barrel without sitting, and goes back to her lantern. Nobody in the crowd is drifting closer. Nobody he can see, anyway.

The cat hasn't moved from his boot, but its ears have gone flat and its tail has wrapped tight around its paws. Through the pact bond comes a feeling with no words in it: *warm, old, hers* — the same smell as the coin at his own throat. Under that is something sour and newer, like a scratch on a clean thing.

Tobin squares the deck with a snap and puts on a good imitation of a grin. "Arrangement with the Lady," he says. "Don't hear that every night on the Crossing. What sort of arrangement does a man make with Tymora that keeps him off a deck, eh?"

I let the question sit while Tobin deals Harl his three cards, and I watch the deal — not to play, just old habit, the way you watch a man's hands when he's nervous. Then I step round to his side of the barrel, close enough that the dockhands won't catch every word, and drop my voice.

"The sort where I lost everything once and she gave it back on her terms. Keeping the deck out of my hands is the cheap part." I nod down at the silver coin without touching it. "That one's hers too. I can feel it from here, and so can you, or you wouldn't have told me a lie that bad. You're not a priest, Tobin, and you don't look like a thief who's happy with his take." I glance, once, at the breast of his coat where his hand went. "So here's how I'd rather this goes. Finish your hand with these two, then you and I walk ten paces down the bridge where the Fist can see us but can't hear us, and you tell me where you got it and what's riding in your coat. I'm not the Watch, and I'm not here to take anything off you. I'm the man the seat was kept for — you said as much yourself."

I keep my tone friendly and tired, like a sergeant giving a frightened recruit the easy way out, and I let him see I mean it. The cat stays where it is, watching the coin.
turns.reply:
Tobin deals Harl three cards, face down on the wood: lift, show the queen, drop, shift, shift, shift. James watches the dealer's hands the way some men watch weather. Tobin is good, better than a barrel on a bridge pays for, but tonight his rhythm is off. On the second shift his little finger lifts too early and James sees the queen go under instead of left. Harl taps the right-hand card with total confidence. It's a two of cups. He swears, Bede laughs, and the coins go to Tobin's side of the barrel.

While Tobin scoops them up, James steps round to his side and speaks low enough that the dockhands only hear a murmur under the eel-seller's shouting. He says his piece in a tired, friendly voice, the one an old sergeant uses on a recruit who's been caught sleeping on watch and expects a flogging. As he talks, his eyes go once to the breast of the green coat and then back to Tobin's face.

Something in Tobin gives way. It isn't the words so much as the voice, the first one in a while that hasn't asked anything of him. His shoulders drop by an inch. He looks at the coin, then at James, and wets his lips.

"Game's closed, lads," he says, louder, and pushes Harl's lost stake back across the wood to him. "House is feeling generous. Off you go."

Harl stares at the coins, then at Tobin, and decides not to argue with free money. Bede is already up and backing away. Before he leaves he takes one last look at James, the look you'd give a man walking toward a dog that hasn't barked yet.

Tobin sweeps up the deck. He doesn't pick the silver coin up straight away. First he flicks it face down with the back of a card, like a man turning over a hot coal, and only then pinches it up and drops it into a side pocket. The cat's head follows the pocket.

They walk the ten paces. James stops where a gap between two stalls opens onto the river and the railing is damp under his hand. From here the Basilisk Gate is in plain view, and so is Sergeant Varn's lantern. The sergeant looks up once and sees two men standing apart from the crowd. She keeps her eyes on them a moment longer than she needs to, then turns back to her queue.

"She gave it me," Tobin says, low and quick, as though the words have been piling up behind his teeth for weeks. "Not the Lady, friend, a woman. Grey. Grey cloak, grey gloves, voice like she's reading you a bedtime story. Spring, it was. She says, you deal on the Crossing, you see everyone coming in off the Way. Put this out face down every night. If it turns up its face on its own, you mark the man. Tell me what he looks like, where he's drinking, how he's playing. A gold a head." He laughs, and nothing in it is funny. "A gold a head for telling a lady who's lucky. What's the harm in that, I thought."

His hand goes to the breast of the coat again. This time he opens the lapel and tilts it toward the lamp. Names are written on the inside of the lining in a cramped, careful hand, the ink feathered where it soaked into the cloth. There are seven of them. Three have a single line drawn through.

"Corwin Dray." His fingertip touches the first struck name and pulls away. "Won forty gold at dice in the Blushing Mermaid, and I told her so. Six days on he comes up under the Grey Harbour quay with a copper in his teeth. The Fist calls it drink." His finger moves down the lining. "Mattis Orle, the same. And this one, I never got his name, just *Amn boy, red cap*. Same again. I started writing them down after Dray, so I'd... so somebody'd know. In case."

He closes the coat and holds it shut with both hands.

"I see her tonight. Near midnight, same as always, under the bridge at the Rock end where the stairs go down to the water. She'll ask did it turn. And it turned for you, friend. Turned the moment you came off the road. I've never seen it go that quick." He swallows. "So you tell me, since you're the one the seat was kept for. What am I meant to say to her?"

I let out a breath through my nose and look out at the water for a moment before I answer. Three men with coppers in their teeth. Paid to the sea.

"You tell her the truth, Tobin. All of it that she'd learn anyway." I turn back to him. "A man came in off the Way at dusk, alone, soldier's cloak, Tethyrian patch, with a cat. Coin turned the moment he set foot on the bridge, fastest you've ever seen. He wouldn't sit, said he had an arrangement with the Lady, and asked where he could find a bed and a drink in the Lower City. You sent him to the Elfsong. That's where he'll be." I tap the rail. "That's all true, so you won't have to act it. Lie to a woman like that and she'll smell it, and then it's your name next on that lining — I'd rather she keeps thinking you're a gold-a-head fool who writes nothing down."

I keep my voice low and even. "Two things, quick, before I go through the gate. Does she come alone to the stairs, or does she have someone standing off? And how does she pay you — coin from her own hand, or does she keep her gloves on?"

While he answers, I'm already looking at the Rock end of the bridge — where the stairs would be, what overlooks them, where a man could sit in the dark and watch a meeting without being part of it. The cat gets a thought down the bond: *tonight you go first, and you go quiet.*
turns.reply:
James lets the breath out through his nose and looks at the river for a while. The Chionthar runs black under the bridge, carrying lamplight in pieces. Three men with coppers in their teeth.

When he turns back and says his piece, Tobin listens like a man being read his own sentence and finding it shorter than he feared. As the story goes on his mouth moves a little, repeating it: *soldier's cloak, Tethyrian patch, a cat, the Elfsong*. At *arrangement with the Lady* he flinches.

"She'll like that," he says. "The arrangement. She'll like that a lot, and I'll be honest, I don't like that she'll like it." He rubs his jaw. "But it's true, and I can say a true thing without my face doing anything. Yeah. Yeah, all right."

Then James asks his two questions, and Tobin answers fast. He's had them in his head for weeks with nobody to ask.

"Alone on the stairs. Always. She comes down from the top, not up from the water, and she stands two steps above me so I'm looking up at her. But there's a boat." He keeps his voice down even though nobody is near. "Every time. A little skiff under the first arch, tied off to the footing, lantern hooded. Man at the oars, or maybe more than one. I never see a face, just a shape and an oar resting. She never looks at it, and that's how I know it's hers." He swallows. "Water's right there, see. That's the bit I think about."

"Gloves stay on. Grey kid, buttoned at the wrist. She's never once touched my hand. The gold comes out of a little drawstring purse, and she tips it into my palm from above, the way you'd feed a dog you don't want licking you." His fingers twitch toward his side pocket, where the old silver coin is, and stop short. "And she always asks the same three things, same order. Where's he drinking. What did he win. Is he still winning." He looks at James and works it out. "You didn't win anything, friend. You didn't play. She'll ask, and I'll have to say *nothing*, and I don't know what she makes of a man the coin turns for who won't sit at a table."

While Tobin talks, James studies the Rock end of the bridge.

Wyrm's Rock rises out of the middle of the Crossing, a squat fortress sitting on an island of black stone, its walls lit by a few high windows. Where the street of shops meets the Rock's footing, about three hundred feet off, there's a gap between a rope-maker's and a shuttered eel stall. A single lamp on an iron arm hangs over it, and the top of a stone stair drops away under the lamp into the dark. James can't see the landing from here. The bridge's edge and the curve of the footing hide it. He can see what's above it, though. The rope-maker has a loft with a hoist-beam and a hatch half open. The roof of the eel stall is flat, tarred and low, with a stack of crates behind it. And under the bridge itself, where the first great arch springs from the Rock, there's a dark line along the stone that could be a ledge, or a drain, or nothing. Anyone who wanted to watch the stairs from above would pick the loft or the stall roof. Anyone who wanted to watch from the water would already be in a boat.

James sends his thought down the bond. The answer isn't a feeling of obedience, and it doesn't feel like fear either. It's lower and warmer than either: *yes*, with the sense of a body settling onto its haunches. Something under it has been waiting since the road to be let off the leash. The cat's tail unwraps from its paws and the tip of it starts, very slowly, to twitch.

At the gate, Sergeant Varn waves a cart of onions through without looking at it. She's looking past it, at the railing.

Tobin follows her glance, then pulls his coat tighter. "You're going in, then. Elfsong." He says it almost as a question, like a man checking his lines before he goes on. "And she's going to come looking for you there, because I told her to. That's — you know that's what you're doing, yeah? You're putting yourself on the barrel."

"I know what I'm doing. I've been bait before — in Tethyr we called it a picket." I give him a half-smile that doesn't reach anything. "Somebody's paying the sea with men the Lady smiled on. I'm her envoy, and I came here to find out how I serve. I think I just did."

I push off the rail. "About the winning. Say it plain — he didn't play, so he didn't win. That's the truth and it'll trouble her more than any lie would. Let her chew on it." I glance at the lining of his coat. "And Tobin — after tonight, that coat goes in a chest and you buy a new one. Keep the gold she gives you in a separate purse and don't spend it; you may need to show somebody where it came from one day. If anything goes wrong on those stairs, don't run along the bridge. Run *up*, toward the gate and the lanterns. She's got a boat; she hasn't got the Fist."

I don't tell him I'll be watching. A frightened man looks where he knows a friend is sitting, and I want his eyes on her and nowhere else.

"Go deal another hour. Act like a man who just had a dull conversation with a tired soldier." I nod toward the gate. "Elfsong, then. If I'm ever in the seat, I'll say Tobin sent me."

I walk back into the queue and let Sergeant Varn get a good look at my papers — the Tethyrian pay slip, my own face, the cat at my heel — a man coming into the city alone and above-board, exactly as the story goes. Once I'm through the Basilisk Gate, my plan is simple: find the Elfsong, take a room under my own name, leave the pack and the crossbow there where a curious eye can find them, eat something — and well before midnight come back out to the Crossing wearing a different face, to sit on the roof of that eel stall with a cat on the crates behind me and a view of the stairs.
turns.reply:
James's half-smile lands on Tobin like a cold hand. The dealer looks at him for a long moment, and whatever he'd been about to say goes unsaid.

"A picket," he repeats. Then he listens to the rest, and James can see him storing each piece away like a card palmed for later. "He didn't play, so he didn't win. Coat in a chest. Her gold in its own purse, don't touch it. Up, not along." He nods once at each, nodding too fast. "Up to the lanterns. Yeah. I can do up."

He pulls the green coat straight and runs a hand down the front, over the names, and for a moment he looks less like a dealer than a man who has just been told what to do with his hands at a funeral. "Tobin sent me," he says. "You say that at the Elfsong and they'll laugh you out the door, friend. Nobody's ever taken my word for anything." Something close to a real smile crosses his face and goes. "Go on, then. I've got an hour of dull to act."

He goes back to his barrel. By the time James reaches the end of the queue, Tobin is shuffling under the lamp and calling the Lady's name to passers-by in the same easy patter as before. If you didn't know to look, you'd never see his eyes go once to the Rock end of the bridge.

The queue moves slowly. A carter ahead of James argues about a bale of hides the Fist want to open. Behind him a tiefling woman with two children stands very still and very straight, the way people stand when they've been through checkpoints before. The lamps are all lit along the Crossing now. The river below has gone from black to a deeper black, and the smell of fried dough drifts over everything. The cat walks at his heel with its tail up again, but its ears keep swivelling back toward the Rock.

It's a quarter of an hour before James reaches the lantern.

Up close, Sergeant Odessa Varn is older than she looked from the railing. She's grey at the temples, with a nose that has been broken at least once and set by someone in a hurry. Her tabard is clean and her boots are not. She takes the Tethyrian pay slip, tilts it to the light and reads every line. Then she looks at his face, at the patch on his cloak, and down at the cat.

"Zaranda's scouts," she says. It isn't a question. She folds the slip and holds it a moment longer than she needs to before handing it back. "Business in the city?"

She doesn't wait long for the answer. Her eyes have already gone past his shoulder, down the bridge to the barrel under the lamp.

"You stood with Leck a good while," she says. "Didn't put down a copper. I watched." Her voice stays flat and low, pitched under the noise of the queue so it reaches only him. "What did he want with you?"

The Fist private beside her goes on poking at the tiefling woman's bundle and isn't listening. The Basilisk Gate stands open behind her, and the Lower City climbs away beyond it into lamplight and smoke.

James tucks the pay slip back inside the cloak. Varn watches his hands do it and then looks at his face while he talks. Her expression doesn't change. Behind her the private has finished with the tiefling woman's bundle and is retying it badly.

It doesn't work. James has said a mostly true thing in a tired voice a hundred times, but this time the sergeant has been standing at the lantern the whole evening and watching him.

He steps aside. The tiefling woman brings her children up to the light. Varn reads the woman's paper in the time it takes to breathe twice, says "Through," and the family goes under the arch without looking back. Then the sergeant turns back to James.

"Beds and meals take a minute." She keeps her voice flat and low. "You were at that rail the time it takes to burn a candle down a finger. He opened his coat to you, under the lamp. Men don't do that to show you where the Elfsong is."

She doesn't sound angry. She sounds like someone counting the same things a second time.

"Is Leck trouble." She repeats it as if she's checking it for weight. "Leck's a sharp with clever hands and no spine. Never been trouble in his life." She stops there a moment. "Some of the men who sit at his barrel. Them I've seen again. Once each. Not standing up."

The private is listening now. Varn doesn't look round at him. "Rivers, see to the cart," she says, and he goes off to see to the cart.

"You asked whose lantern to run toward. Mine's this one. I'm on it till the midnight bell, and after that I'm somewhere I'll decide later." She holds out her hand, palm up, as if he still owed her a paper. "So. One soldier to another, since that's how you want it. What's written in his coat?"

Varn keeps her hand out while he talks, and then she lowers it slowly, as if she's forgotten it was there. She doesn't interrupt. When he gets to *Corwin Dray* her jaw sets and stays set. "Fourth," Varn says back to him. She doesn't add anything to it.

When he explains the cat she looks down at it, and the cat looks up at her the way it looks at everything, as if it has already decided and is waiting for her to catch up.

"Taps on the stone." Her mouth moves at one corner. It isn't quite a smile. "If it sits on my boot and won't get off, I'll take that for the cellar." Then her eyes go back to the queue and her voice goes flat again. "Well out. I heard you."

She lifts the lantern an inch, which is all the dismissal anyone at the Basilisk Gate gets, and James goes under the arch.

The gate passage is cold and smells of wet stone and horse. It's twenty paces of echo, and then the Lower City opens out in front of him all at once. Streets drop downhill in steps and switchbacks, roof below roof, lamplit windows stacked on lamplit windows, all the way down to a dark band of masts at the bottom where the harbour is. After the bridge the noise is different. It isn't hawkers any more. It's doors and shutters, a cart's iron tyres on cobbles, somebody practising a fiddle badly behind a wall. The air still smells of tar and fish, and under that coal smoke and bread.

The cat walks at his heel for the first street. On the second it starts making little detours: into a doorway, along the bottom of a wall, nose to a gutter grate. Through the bond comes a flood of smells all at once: *fish, fish, rat, old fish, a dog that's gone, fish.* It sounds overwhelmed and very pleased about it.

The first lamplighter James passes is an old man on a short ladder with a hooked brass pole. He's coaxing a wick at the corner of a street that seems to be called Steephill, judging by the cobbles. He has a grey beard and a waxed leather apron, and sticks of tallow are tucked behind both ears like a clerk's pens. He hears the question and doesn't come down.

"Elfsong." He gets the flame to catch, lowers the glass and only then looks round. He takes in the cloak, the pack, the cat. "Straight down three turnings, past the chandler with the blue door, then left where it smells of hops. You'll hear it before you see it, this time of night. Talking, not singing. Singing's later." He climbs down a rung. "Go now and you'll get a stool. Go after the bell and you'll stand, and some fool from the ships will weep on you about his mother."

Halfway down the second turning a boy with a satchel of broadsheets is working his corner in a cracked, carrying voice. *"Baldur's Mouth, Baldur's Mouth! Elturel grain barges held at Wyrm's Rock, tolls in dispute! Grand Duke speaks on the Outer City! House Vell's Gull's Wing in from Calimport two days early, not a reef nor a squall the whole way, Lady bless her! Baldur's Mouth!"* A man in a merchant's coat stops, buys a sheet and mutters something to his companion about Vell's luck being the only steady thing on the coast. Then they're past.

The chandler's door is blue, as promised. The left turn does smell of hops. A brewery's back wall runs along one side of the lane, warm to walk beside.

The Elfsong stands at the end of the lane, where it widens into a small cobbled yard. It's an old building, older than its neighbours, three storeys of dark timber and grey stone. The upper floors lean out over the lower one, and the windows are full of yellow light. Someone has carved a leaf-and-vine pattern into the lintel over the door, and long years of hands have worn it smooth. The lamplighter was right: James hears it from the yard. There's the low roar of a full common room, a laugh going up, crockery knocking together.

He goes in, and the warmth hits him like a wall. The room is long and low-beamed, a fire at one end and the bar at the other. It's busy without being packed: sailors, a table of dwarves in leather aprons, two Fist off duty with their tabards folded on the bench beside them, a pair of well-dressed young men losing at dice in a corner. James's eyes go there, and he makes them come away again. There's a stair up to the rooms at the back. One stool is still empty at the end of the bar.

Behind the bar a big woman of fifty or so is drying a tankard with a cloth that has seen better years. She has a red face, iron-grey hair pinned up with what looks like a knitting needle, and forearms like a stevedore's. She sees the pack before she sees the man, and the cat before either. The cat has walked in as if it had a room booked and has gone straight to the fire.

"That yours?" she says, nodding at the hearth, where the cat is already turning round twice on the warmest stone. "Hesper. I keep this house." She sets the tankard down. "You've come off the road with that pack, so it's a bed you're after or I'm a gnome. Room, or just a drink first while you make your mind up?"

turns.message:
"Mine, and he's already decided, so I suppose that settles it." I shrug the pack off and set it against the bar. "A room, Hesper. Two nights to start, and I'll pay ahead. James Worgen — write it in your book plain, I'm not hiding from anyone." I put the coin on the wood. "And whatever's hot, with bread, and a pint of something that isn't the sailors' choice. I've been eating hardtack since Beregost."

While she fetches the key I take the empty stool and let my back rest against the bar, facing the room, the way a tired man would who's done walking for the day. "One thing more, if you don't mind a stranger's question. The boy on the corner was shouting about a ship — House Vell's *Gull's Wing*, in from Calimport two days early and not a squall the whole way. Man in the street called Vell's luck the only steady thing on the coast." I turn the tankard she sets down. "Is that true, or is it just the Mouth selling sheets? I ask because I've a goddess who takes an interest in luck, and I'd like to know who else in this town is on good terms with her."
turns.reply:
Hesper looks at the cat, which has settled on the warmest stone with its back to the room, then at James. She snorts.

"They do decide." She lays the cloth over her shoulder, takes the coin off the wood and turns it once under the lamp before it vanishes into her apron. "Two nights and tonight's plate, that's your gold, near enough. Breakfast is extra and the lamp oil's mine." Under the bar is a ledger with a cracked spine. She opens it, licks a pencil stub, and writes *James Worgen* in big square letters with no flourish, the way he asked. Then she looks at it. "Plain. Not many ask for plain. Usually it's *Smith* and a wink."

She reaches behind her to a board of hooks and takes down an iron key on a wooden tag. Six notches have been cut into the tag's edge with a knife. "Six. Top of the stair, second floor, end of the passage. The window looks on the yard, not the lane, so the brewery carts won't wake you. Bolt's sound. Don't let the cat on the bolster, the last one shed like a sheep."

She shouts something at the kitchen hatch. A minute later a bowl lands in front of James, big enough to wash a hand in: mutton and barley stew with a skin of fat on top, and a heel of brown bread with the crust still crackling. The pint that follows is dark, almost black, with a head the colour of old ivory. "The dwarves' brown," she says, and nods down the room at the table in leather aprons. "They brew it in Gond's quarter and won't drink anything else. The sailors' choice is piss with ambition. You're welcome."

James turns his back to the bar and faces the room. Hesper goes back to her tankards and listens to his question about Vell with her eyes on the cloth. When he gets to *a goddess who takes an interest in luck* she stops drying for a moment.

"Vell." She sets the tankard down. "It's not the Mouth selling sheets. Not this time. The *Gull's Wing*, the *Margery*, the one with the gold on her stern, can't think of her name. Two years now and not one of them lost a day to weather. Not one." She holds up a thick finger. "You get sailors in here at the turn of the season, crying because they've lost a month off Tethyr in fog, or they've been blown halfway to the Nelanther. Never a Vell crew. They come in early and dry and they drink like men who've got paid twice." She picks the cloth back up. "Every deckhand on the quays wants a Vell berth now. Half of them would sell their mothers for one, or I'm a gnome."

She gives the tankard another pass and talks lower.

"There's two ways folk tell it. One is old Cassandor Vell hires good captains and pays for good charts, and that's all. The other..." She tilts her head toward the harbour, somewhere past the wall. "The Water Queen's women don't like it. Umberlee's lot. They come round the quays for the tithe like everybody's mother-in-law, and the talk is Vell's ships stopped paying a while back. And a ship that stops paying the Queen ought to be meeting weather, not dodging it. So either Vell's found a better priest or the sea's not keeping her books." She shrugs her big shoulders. "That's sailor talk. I don't make it, I just pour it."

Down the room, one of the well-dressed young men at the dice table throws, whoops, and slaps the table. His friend groans and pushes a little stack of silver across. The winner is maybe twenty, with a velvet collar and a flushed face, and he's been winning for a while from the look of the pile in front of him. Hesper watches him over James's shoulder with no expression at all.

"As for who's on good terms with your Lady," she says, "the Lady's Hall's up top, behind the inner wall, if you can get past the Watch. Big doors, lots of gilt. They'll talk to you about luck as long as you like, provided you put something in the bowl first." Her eyes go back to the dice table. "And down here, it's whoever's winning tonight. Changes by the hour."

By the fire the cat has lifted its head off its paws. It isn't looking at the dice. It's looking at the young man's velvet collar, and through the bond comes something faint and thin, there and gone, like the smell of a struck match in another room: *hers. Warm.* Then nothing, and the cat puts its chin back down.

The stew is hot. Somewhere upstairs a door closes. It's not much past half eight, and the midnight bell is a long way off yet.

turns.message:
I eat, because a soldier eats when there's food, and I watch the dice table over the rim of the dwarves' brown.

"Good stew," I tell Hesper, and mean it. Then, lower, not looking away from the corner: "The boy in the velvet collar. He's been winning a while, and he's the kind that'll walk home alone counting it. Who is he, and does he come in often?" I tear the bread. "I ask for the same reason I asked about Vell. Four men came through the Basilisk Gate this summer on a lucky streak, and all four came up off Grey Harbour quay with a copper in their teeth. The Fist calls it drink. I don't. If that lad's the next, I'd rather he was somebody's son with a name than a line in Baldur's Mouth."

I let her chew on that, and down the bond I tell the cat: *stay by the fire. If the collar leaves before I do, you follow him to his door and come back. Nothing more.*
turns.reply:
James eats the way a soldier eats when he doesn't know where the next meal is coming from: steadily, without fuss, the bread used as a spoon once the spoon stops being enough. The stew is better than it has any right to be at that price. The brown is bitter and smooth and sits in the stomach like a banked fire.

He watches the corner over the rim of the tankard.

The young man in the velvet collar throws right-handed. Before every throw his left hand goes to his waistcoat, to the little pocket over the ribs, and presses flat there for a moment before he lets the dice go. He does it every time, without looking and without knowing he does it. James has seen it at a hundred tables, from across the board and in his own hands in the bad years. It's a man touching his luck to make sure it's still there.

"Good stew," he says, and Hesper grunts as if he'd told her the river was wet.

Then he lowers his voice and asks his question. At *four men* her cloth stops. At *a copper in their teeth* she puts the tankard down on the bar, carefully, and leaves her hand on it.

She looks down the room at the corner for a long moment before she answers.

"Teo Askew." She keeps her voice under the noise of the room. "His father writes cover on cargoes at the Counting House. Old Askew would skin him if he knew where the boy spends his nights." She nods at the groaning friend without naming him. "That's Corrie. Clerk in the same counting-room. Paid to keep an eye on him, I'd guess, and doing it badly."

She picks the cloth up again but doesn't use it.

"Teo's been in since winter. Lost all spring, regular as rent. Corrie won off him most nights and bought the drinks with it." Her mouth flattens. "Ten days back it turned round. He hasn't lost a night since. Not one." She lets that sit. "His father sends a link-boy for him at the eleventh bell. Last week Teo started giving the boy a silver to go home without him."

Down the room Corrie pushes the last of his stack across and holds up both hands. Teo laughs, flushed and delighted. His left hand goes to his waistcoat pocket again.

"Corwin Dray drank here," Hesper says. "Twice. Loud man, paid in silver, sang badly." She looks at James then, straight on, the first time she's looked at his face and not his pack or his cat. "He could drink those dwarves under their own table and walk a plank home after. Drink, they said." She snorts, and there's nothing amused in it.

She leans in a little over the bar.

"Hear me. I don't know what you are and I'm not asking. But nobody leaves my door to end up under a quay, and nobody gets hurt on my floor either. Whatever you're about, you don't start it in here."

By the fire the cat hasn't moved, but its ears have turned toward the corner and stayed there. When James's order reaches it down the bond, the answer comes back low and settled: *yes.* A body flattening on warm stone, eyes half shut and not asleep at all. Then something else slips in under the yes that he didn't ask for: a lantern on a hook, the smell of wet stone and horse, a pair of dirty boots. *Both,* the cat seems to say. *Don't forget the other one.*

At the dice table Corrie is half out of his chair. "I'm out, Teo. I'm *out*. I've rent."

"One more." Teo is already scooping up the dice. "One more, Corrie, come on. I can't lose tonight. I *can't*."

It's just short of nine. Above the noise of the room, somewhere in the beams, nothing sings yet.

turns.message:
I nod to Hesper — understood, not on her floor — and finish the brown. Down the bond: *When I stand, go to the gate. Her lantern. Six taps, then come straight back here and watch the collar.*

Then I walk down the room with the empty tankard in my hand like a man heading for the bar's far end, and stop at the dice table instead. I don't sit, and I keep my hands well clear of the dice.

"Corrie, is it? Go home. You've rent, and he'll still be winning tomorrow." I say it kindly, like someone who's stood where Corrie's standing. Then to Teo, easy, a little amused: "Ten days without a losing night. I know the feeling — I had three weeks of it once in Athkatla, and I'd have told you I couldn't lose either." I nod at his left hand, which is resting on his waistcoat again. "What is it you keep touching, there? A coin, I'd wager — old silver, the Lady's face on it, warm when it's got no business being warm." I let him see I'm not guessing. "I'm not after your money, lad; I don't play. I'd just like to know who gave it to you, because I met a man tonight who had the twin of it, and he was more frightened than you are."
turns.reply:
James meets Hesper's eye and gives her a short nod: understood, not on her floor. She holds his look a moment longer, then goes back to her tankard. He finishes the brown in two long pulls.

Down the bond: *When I stand, go to the gate. Her lantern. Six taps, then come straight back here and watch the collar.*

The answer is a long, lazy stretch on the hearthstone, claws out and in. When James gets off the stool, the cat is already up. It doesn't hurry. It walks the length of the room along the foot of the wall, past the dwarves' boots, waits by the door until a sailor opens it, and goes out under his legs into the yard. The sailor looks down, says "Huh," and comes in.

James walks down the room with the empty tankard in his hand, like a man heading for the far end of the bar, and stops at the dice table instead. He stays on his feet. His hands stay well clear of the wood.

Corrie looks up at *Go home*. He's thin and ink-fingered, with a clerk's stoop and a face that has spent the evening doing sums it didn't like. For a moment he looks like a man who has been offered a rope.

"I — yes." He's already reaching for his coat. Then his eyes go to Teo, and he stops with one arm in the sleeve. "I'm meant to... his father'd want..." He doesn't finish. He looks at the stranger, at Teo, at the door, and works out what staying would cost him. "The link-boy's coming at eleven. He'll see him home." He says it to nobody in particular, like a man reading back an entry he knows is wrong. "Goodnight, Teo."

Teo doesn't look at him. He's looking at James, and the delighted flush has gone stiff at the edges.

James says his piece easily, a little amused: Athkatla, three weeks, *I couldn't lose either*. Teo's mouth twitches at that, half a smile, the look of a boy hearing an older man admit to something. Then James nods at the left hand resting on the waistcoat and names it: *a coin, old silver, the Lady's face, warm when it's got no business being warm.*

The hand doesn't move off the pocket. It presses harder.

Then Teo laughs. It's short and surprised, and it comes out of him before he can stop it.

"*Silver.*" He glances over his shoulder at the room. Corrie is gone through the door, and nobody else is watching, so he leans in. "Then your frightened man's got the cheap one, sir. Nobody *gave* me anything. I paid for mine. More than Corrie earns in a season, and Father's going to wonder where it went out of my allowance, so don't — " He stops. The thing he'd been about to say about his father goes back unsaid.

He doesn't want to tell a stranger anything. What he wants even more is for somebody to *see*, and nobody has seen it in ten days. The left hand slips two fingers into the waistcoat pocket and draws the coin halfway out, low against his ribs where only James can see it in the shadow of the table.

It's gold, and newer than old. The Lady's face is there, smiling, the same face that hangs on the cord at James's throat. Something has been struck over it afterwards, a second, heavier blow that has pushed the gold up in ridges across her brow: two branching tines, one on each side of her head, like a crown of bare twigs.

James doesn't need a temple to tell him what that is. Any priest of the Lady, any of her envoys, any gambler who ever spat over his shoulder after a bad roll knows the black antlers. Beshaba. The Maid of Misfortune, the Lady's sister and her enemy, stamped on top of Tymora's smile like a boot on a face.

At his throat, his own coin gives one small cold prickle, the way skin does when someone opens a door behind you.

Teo sees none of it. He's looking at the coin the way he looked at the dice, flushed and fond. "That's just the stamp," he says, and tucks it away and presses it flat. "Southern minting, the man said. Calimport does them like that." His jaw sets in a way that says *the man* is as far as that goes. "I'm not telling you where. If I tell you, you'll go and buy one, and then there'll be two of us, and I don't know if it — " He hasn't got an end for that sentence either.

He picks the dice up and turns them over in his right hand without throwing. His eyes come back to James's face, and for the first time tonight he isn't excited. He sounds young.

"Athkatla," he says. "Your three weeks. How did it stop?"

I pull Corrie's empty chair out a foot and sit on it sideways, back to the wall, so Teo and I are two men talking and not a stranger standing over a table.

"It stopped the way they all stop. One night it wasn't there." I say it flat, without dressing it. "I'd three weeks of money in a strongbox and I put the box on the table because I *couldn't lose*. I lost it in one hand. Then I lost the horse, and the company's share, and a note I'm still carrying from a man who lost worse than me the same night. I was on my knees on a tavern floor in Athkatla praying to a goddess I'd never given a copper to, and that's the only reason I'm sitting here." I touch the cord at my throat. "Mine's silver, lad. Plain. It cost me everything I had and a promise I'm keeping tonight, and it's the only reason I haven't put my hand on your dice."

I nod at his pocket, and drop my voice further. "Now listen, because I'll say this once and then it's yours to do with. That isn't a Calimport stamp. Those ridges over her brow are antlers. Black antlers — her sister's mark, struck over her face. Any priest in the Lady's Hall would tell you the same and then wash his hands. Beshaba doesn't *give* luck, Teo. She lends it, and she collects." I hold his eye. "Four men came through the Basilisk Gate this summer winning like you. All four stopped winning between six and nine days later, face down under Grey Harbour quay with a copper in their teeth. You're on day ten."

I let that land. "I'm not asking for the coin, and I'm not asking for the name tonight. Two things only. When the link-boy comes at eleven, you go home with him — you don't buy him off, and you don't walk alone. And tomorrow, sober, in daylight, you find me here and tell me who sold it to you, so I can go and look at the man instead of at you. That's all. Do that, and whatever your father wonders about the allowance, he won't be wondering it at a funeral."

James pulls Corrie's chair out a foot and sits on it sideways with his back to the wall. Now they're two men talking over a table, not a stranger standing over one. Teo's eyes follow him down, and some of the stiffness goes out of the boy's shoulders.

James tells it flat. Teo's face goes through a few things while he listens. At *I put the box on the table* the boy almost smiles, the way you smile at a story you know the end of. At *the horse* he stops smiling. At *on my knees on a tavern floor* he looks away, toward the fire, where the cat isn't any more. Then James nods at the pocket, lowers his voice, and says *antlers*.

Teo's left hand comes off the waistcoat as if the cloth had gone hot. A moment later it goes back, and stays there.

*Six and nine days. You're on day ten.*

The boy is very still. Somebody laughs at the bar, and one of the dwarves bangs a tankard down. Teo doesn't hear any of it.

The boy doesn't argue. He lets the dice drop out of his right hand onto the wood, and he doesn't look at what they show. Then he turns the pocket over in his head the way he was turning the dice, and James watches him decide. He's frightened, but he's more ashamed of being frightened in front of a man who has just told him about a tavern floor.

"Eleven," Teo says. "Hob. The link-boy's called Hob. He's twelve, he's got a lantern bigger than he is." He swallows. "I gave him a silver on Tuesday and he looked at me like I'd hit him. He tells Father everything else, he'd have told him that if I hadn't..." He doesn't finish. "I'll go with Hob."

He pulls his stack of silver toward him and starts putting it into his purse a coin at a time. His hands are steadier with something to do.

"Tomorrow." He says the word as if he's agreeing to a price. "Not tonight. Not in here." His eyes go round the room once: the sailors, the off-duty Fist, the dwarves, Hesper behind the bar drying a tankard with her eyes on nothing. "Midday. Father goes up to the Counting House at the tenth bell and doesn't come down till dark. I'll come here. I'll tell you where, and who. It isn't..." He stops, and presses his lips shut on the rest. "Tomorrow."

The last of the silver goes into the purse. He pulls the drawstring tight, then sits with both hands flat on the table, the left one nowhere near his waistcoat. It costs him something to keep it there, and James can see how much.

Down the bar, Hesper has stopped pretending to dry anything. She looks at the empty chair James is sitting in, then at the boy putting his winnings away before the eleventh bell, and gives one short nod to nobody. Then she goes back to her cloth.

Teo looks up. His face is young and pale under the flush.

"Sir. Tonight." His voice drops to almost nothing. "Do I keep it on me? Or does that... does it matter, if I'm not playing?"

turns.message:
I take a moment with that, because it deserves an honest answer and not a quick one.

"I don't know, lad. I'll tell you what I think, and you'll hear that it's thinking." I keep my voice low. "A coin like that isn't just luck. It's how they *find* you — one of the four never sat at any table that was being watched, and they found him anyway. So I don't think you can take it off and be rid of it tonight, and I don't want you throwing it in the harbour either; the sea is the one who's been collecting. And don't hand it to me. I'm already standing on the barrel, and I'd rather not stand there holding two."

I lean in. "So: it stays in your pocket till Hob gets you home. Then it goes in your father's iron box with the cargo papers, under his roof and his lock, and you sleep in another room from it. Don't sell it, don't lend it, don't show it to anyone who asks after it — and if anyone does ask, a woman especially, grey cloak, grey gloves, voice like a bedtime story, you say nothing and walk toward lanterns. Bring it to me tomorrow at midday wrapped in a cloth, and we'll take it up to the Lady's Hall together and let a priest tell us both what it is."

I stand and push the chair back where Corrie left it. "You did well tonight. Better than I did in Athkatla." A nod to his purse. "Count that in daylight, and don't double it."
turns.reply:
James takes a moment before he answers, and Teo waits. He doesn't fidget. His hands stay flat on the table.

The boy follows the reasoning link by link: it's how they find you, the sea is the one who's been collecting, I'm already standing on the barrel. At *don't hand it to me* something crosses his face that might be relief, and might be the opposite. He had half-expected to be asked for it, and he had a refusal ready. Now he has nothing to do with it.

At *your father's iron box* his chin comes up.

"Not Father's box." He says it quickly. "He opens it every morning before the tenth bell and counts what's in it, paper by paper. He'd find it in a breath, and then I'd be explaining a gold coin with —" he lowers his voice, "— with *that* on it, to a man who writes cover on ships." He hunts for something better and finds it. "My writing desk locks. Brass lock, my own key. It's in the room at the end, the one nobody sleeps in since my sister married. I'll put it there and sleep in mine." A short breath. "Another room. You're right. I wouldn't have thought of that."

He takes the rest the way he took the silver into his purse, one piece at a time. Don't sell it, don't lend it, don't show it. When James describes the grey cloak, the grey gloves and *a voice like a bedtime story*, Teo's eyes go to the door, the way they did before, and come back.

"Nobody's asked," he says. "Nobody knows I've got it, except the man who sold it." He stops. That's as close as he'll come tonight. "Lanterns. Yes."

Then James says *the Lady's Hall*, and Teo looks at him properly again.

"Up top? Together?" A ghost of the flushed boy comes back for a moment. "The Watch'll stop you at the Wyrm Gate in that cloak, sir. They stop everybody who looks like he's walked somewhere." He considers it, and something like pride comes into his face, the pleasure of having something to offer. "They don't stop me. I go up on Father's business twice a month with his papers. If I say you're with me, they'll grumble and let you through." He nods once, firmly, like a man shaking on a price. "Midday. Wrapped in a cloth. And then up the hill."

James stands and pushes Corrie's chair back where it was. *You did well tonight. Better than I did in Athkatla.*

Teo goes red to the ears. It isn't the flush of winning. He looks down at the purse in front of him as if he'd forgotten it was there.

"Count it in daylight," he says quietly, half to himself, the way a clerk reads a figure back. "Don't double it."

He doesn't pick up the dice again. When James turns away, the boy is sitting with his back straight and both hands on the wood, looking at the door, waiting for a twelve-year-old with a lantern bigger than he is.

At the bar Hesper has a fresh tankard in her hand that she isn't drying. She watches James come back up the room and says nothing. She sets the tankard down upside down on the shelf, the way you put away something you won't need tonight.

It's about twenty-five past nine. The hearthstone by the fire is still empty. The cat hasn't come back yet.

If Hob's late, or if anyone else comes asking after Teo Askew before then, I'd take it as a kindness if you remembered you never heard the name." Then up the stair to six. I bolt the door, check the window on the yard and how far the drop is, and lay things out the way a careless man would: the pack open on the bed, the crossbow and bolts propped in the corner where anyone looking in would see them, the regimental pay slip on the table under the lamp with my name plain on it. The promissory note and the deck stay on me. So do the rod, the cloak, the coin and the two potions.

I sit on the bed with my back to the wall and wait for the cat, reaching down the bond for it as it comes back from the gate — I want to know Varn got her six taps, and I want to know if anything on the bridge has changed since dusk. When it's back and settled, I'll put on another face before I go down: a Rivington boatman, grey in the beard, a dockhand's canvas jacket in place of the Tethyrian cloak, nothing anyone would look at twice on the Crossing after dark. The cloak's enchantment comes with me whatever it looks like.
turns.reply:
James gives Hesper a nod on his way past the bar and stops just long enough to say it under the noise. She hears him out with the cloth still in her hand. His fingers go to his purse, and before the coin is clear of it she says, "Put that away."

She doesn't look up from the tankard. "Hob's never late. That boy'd come through a fire with that lantern." She turns the tankard a quarter turn and wipes it again. "And I don't know any Askews. Never had one in."

That's the end of it. James goes up the stair.

The stair is old and narrow and turns twice. Every tread creaks a different note. The Boots of Elvenkind make no sound on any of them, so only the wood talks. At the second floor a passage runs back along the house under a sloping ceiling, with doors on one side and the smell of lamp oil and old beeswax. Six is at the end, as she said. The key turns hard, and the bolt inside is a good iron one that goes home with a solid clack.

The room is about what two nights' money buys. There's a narrow bed with a bolster, a washstand with a chipped jug, a table and one chair, a lamp, a row of pegs, and a small rag rug that someone once cared about. The ceiling comes down at a slant over the bed, low enough that a tall man would learn about it in the night.

He goes to the window first. It's a casement with small leaded panes and a latch that sticks before it gives. Below is the yard he crossed coming in: cobbles, the worn lintel's lamp throwing a yellow fan over the door, and the mouth of the hops-smelling lane at the far side. It's a long drop to the cobbles, fifteen feet or a bit more, onto stone. A little to the left and about six feet down, though, is the mossy slate roof of a woodshed built against the wall. A man could let himself down onto that from the sill without a rope, and onto a water butt at the corner from there. Nobody is in the yard. A cart stands empty by the brewery wall with its shafts on the ground.

Then he lays out the room the way a careless man would. He opens the pack on the bed and leaves the bedroll half out. The crossbow and the quiver of bolts lean in the corner where the door would show them to anyone who looked in. He spreads the pay slip flat on the table under the lamp, *James Worgen* face up in a regimental clerk's tidy hand. The promissory note and the deck go back inside his jacket, against his ribs. The rod, the cloak, the coin on its cord and the two red potions stay where they are.

He sits on the bed with his back to the wall, under the slope of the ceiling, and reaches down the bond.

For a while there's nothing, only the far, cottony silence of a link stretched past where it can carry. The common room's noise comes up through the floorboards: a laugh, a chair scraping. Somewhere along the passage a door opens and closes. Then, a little before the three-quarter hour, the bond catches like a fish taking a line.

What comes first is a jumble of road, the way it always comes when the cat is moving fast: cobbles, a gutter, the hops wall, and below all of it the cat's pleasure at being out and running with a job to do. Then the memory, pushed at him whole, the way a cat brings you something it's caught. There's lantern heat on its back and boot leather under it, a worn boot that smells of horse and the bridge, and a woman's voice just above. The voice isn't speaking to him. It's counting under its breath along with the tail on the stone, one, two, up to six, and then a seventh beat where the tail stops and nothing comes.

*"Six,"* in that flat checkpoint voice. Then the boot shifts under it, slowly, the way you move a foot when something is sitting on it that you've decided not to kick.

So Varn has her six.

Behind that comes the bridge, seen from the gate at cat height, all legs and wheels and lamplight in a long line. There's Tobin's barrel and its lamp, still lit. Tobin is under it and shuffling, and the smell coming off him is sharper than it was at dusk, like sweat gone cold. Past him, three hundred feet down the Crossing toward the black hump of the Rock, the cat shows him something it noticed because it was different. At dusk a lamp on an iron arm hung over the gap by the rope-maker's. Now there's only the arm. The gap is dark, a missing tooth in the row of lit shopfronts, and the head of the stair is somewhere inside it.

The cat doesn't know what that means, and doesn't pretend to. It only knows the place has changed, so it brings it to him.

Then the common room arrives through its eyes, warm and close: the door, the dwarves' boots, the hearthstone. In the corner, the velvet collar sits straight-backed, both hands on the wood, with no dice in them. The cat turns twice on the warm stone and lies down facing the corner. The bond settles into something low and steady. *Here. Watching.*

James stands, faces the dark window glass and lets the Lady's mask come over him.

It takes a few muttered words and a pass of the hand down the face. Nobody would remember it as anything if they saw it. In the glass, a different man looks back at him. He's a Rivington boatman, broader in the face and older, with grey through a short beard and a nose that has been out in a lot of weather. The Tethyrian cloak is gone. In its place is a dockhand's canvas jacket, tar-stained at the cuffs, with the collar turned up and a knitted cap pulled down. His boots look like boots that have stood in bilge water. The coin on its cord has vanished under a collar that isn't there. Beneath it all, the cloak still hangs from his shoulders, light and real, and the old enchantment in it sits close and quiet as ever.

Below him the common room goes on, loud and yellow. The way down is the stair he came up. It ends at the foot of the room, in full view of the bar and of Hesper, who wrote *James Worgen* in her book an hour ago and has watched everyone who has gone up those stairs tonight. The other way is the window, the woodshed and the yard.

It's about ten to ten.

---

The Mask of Many Faces lets you recast it as often as you like without spending a slot, but it's still a spoken spell with a gesture, so anyone close by can see you do it.*

Down the bond, before I go: *Stay on the collar until the boy with the big lantern takes him out the door. Walk them to their house. Then come to the Crossing — the flat roof of the eel stall by the dark gap, I'll be on it. If you can't find me there, go to the woman's boot at the gate and stay with her.*

I turn the lamp down low — not out — leave the pay slip under it, and work the casement latch. Over the sill, down onto the woodshed slates, the water butt, the cobbles. I cross the yard like a man who's just been round the back to piss, and take the hops lane out.

I don't go to the Rock end first. I go back up to the Basilisk Gate and out through it with the night traffic — a boatman with his cap down, heading home to Rivington, nothing for a sergeant's lantern to stop — and walk the Crossing the way I walked it at dusk, only the other way. Past Tobin's barrel without a glance. I'm looking at that gap by the rope-maker's as I come to it: whether the lamp's glass is broken on the cobbles, or the wick simply pinched out, or the whole thing lifted off its arm; whether anyone is standing in the dark of it; whether the loft hatch above is still half open. I don't stop. A boatman walks past dark places every night.

Then round behind the eel stall, where the crates are, and I take the roof slow and quiet — the boots will keep me silent, and I want to be sure I'm the first one up there. Flat on the tar, cap down, with the stair-head and the first arch below me and most of two hours to lie still in. I've lain in worse.

James turns the lamp down until the flame is a bead of blue at the bottom of the glass. In that light the pay slip lies on the table with his name the only thing on it you can read. He works the casement latch. It sticks, the way he found it, and then gives with a small dry click. The night air comes in cool off the yard, smelling of hops and wet slate.

Down the bond goes the order: *stay on the collar, walk them home, then the eel-stall roof. If I'm not there, her boot.* The answer comes back from the hearthstone below without words, a kind of patience. The cat already knew. It was only waiting for him to say it.

He goes over the sill feet first and hangs at full stretch from the frame for a moment. The woodshed roof is a dark slope under him, nearer than it looked. He lets go. The slates take his weight with a soft grind of moss and nothing louder, and the boots put him down on them the way a hand puts down a cup. He goes along to the corner and down onto the water butt's lid. It booms faintly under him, an empty, wooden sound. Then he's on the cobbles. Nobody in the yard. The cart stands by the brewery wall with its shafts on the ground, and the fan of lamplight from the Elfsong's door lies across the stones without a shadow in it.

He crosses the yard tugging at the front of his jacket like a man who's been round the back, and goes out by the hops lane.

Going up is slower than coming down was. Steephill climbs in steps and switchbacks, and the boatman's body he's wearing would be breathing hard by the second turning. He lets it. The crier boy has gone from his corner. The old lamplighter's work burns all the way up the hill, one lamp per corner.

The Basilisk Gate is still open. Outbound traffic is thin: a carter with an empty wagon, two sailors arm in arm and singing different songs, a woman with a covered basket. Nobody checks anyone going out. Sergeant Varn stands at her lantern on the city side of the arch with a paper in her hand that she isn't reading. James walks past her at six feet, cap down. Her eyes touch him and slide off, a grey-bearded Rivington man going home. She's looking down the bridge toward the Rock, where a gap in the row of lit shopfronts still sits dark.

He walks the Crossing the way he walked it at dusk, the other way round. Most of the hawkers have packed up. The eel-seller who was shouting earlier is gone, and the smell of fried dough has gone cold and stale. Tobin's lamp still burns over the barrel. James passes it at the pace of a man with somewhere to be and keeps his eyes on the cobbles ahead. He hears the cards, the patter, *find the Lady*, a little too loud for a bridge this empty.

Three hundred feet on, the gap by the rope-maker's opens on his left. He doesn't turn his head, only his eyes.

He gets nothing from it. The gap is a slot of black between two lit fronts. At a walking pace, with his eyes on it for three strides and no more, he can make out the iron arm against the lesser dark of the sky and nothing else. He can't tell if the lamp still hangs from it. He can't see the loft hatch, or whether anyone is standing at the top of the stair. If someone is in there, he's walked past them at ten feet without knowing. The dark keeps all of it.

He walks on to the end of the eel stall and turns down the narrow slot behind it. The bridge's edge is here, a low parapet, and past it the Chionthar is black and moving. The crates are where he saw them at dusk, stacked three high against the stall's back wall and smelling strongly of eels. He goes up them quietly. The boots make no sound at all. The top crate does. It rocks under his hand as he puts his weight on it and knocks once against the back of the stall, a hollow wooden *tock* that the shutters swallow.

He freezes there for a breath, then goes on and lies flat on the roof. The tar is still faintly warm from the day. From here, through the gap in the fronts, he can see the top of the stair dropping away into darkness. Past the roof's back edge, if he cranes, there's the dark curve of the Rock's footing and the black mouth of the first arch over the water.

Something moves under him.

It's in the stall, under the boards, a foot from his chest: the scrape of a body sitting up on something hard, then the clink of metal against a tub. A voice comes up through the roof and the shutters. It's young, a girl's, pitched low and rough to sound bigger than it is.

"Who's that." It isn't quite a question. "I heard you. Get off my da's roof." A pause, and a breath drawn in through the teeth. "I've got the gaff, and I'll put it up through the boards, I will. Or I'll scream the Fist down off the gate. Which do you want?"

Somewhere behind him, three hundred feet back up the bridge, Tobin is still calling the Lady to passers-by. Below, the river goes on talking to the stones.

---

As far as he can tell nobody out on the bridge saw him climb. The one person who did notice is a foot below him, holding a gaff.

Someone had pinched the wick and left the lamp hanging. The rope-maker's loft hatch, half open at dusk, was shut tight. Nobody was standing in the dark at the top of the stair. Someone had made the gap dark on purpose and then left it empty.

He doesn't move. Lying flat on the warm tar, he lets the boatman's mutter go down through the boards.

The girl hears him out. She doesn't say a word, but he can hear her breathing, short and fast, close under his chest. At *Rook* nothing changes. At *a boat comes under the first arch* the breathing stops for a moment.

The gold piece slides off his fingers and through the gap at the edge of the shutter. It hits the boards inside with a small bright *tink*, rolls, and stops.

The coin goes still on the boards. For a breath nothing happens. Then the girl lets out a sound that is half a laugh, and James hears wood knock wood as she lays the gaff down on the tubs.

"Gods. A *whole* one." He hears the coin scrape on the boards as she picks it up, then a pause. He can guess she's biting it. "It's real."

When she speaks again she doesn't try to sound bigger than she is, and she sounds about thirteen.

"Rook. All right. I'm Dace." She sniffs. "Da named all of us after fish. Don't." Her voice comes closer to the boards, right under his ear. "You're not a boatman, neither. Boatmen climb like sacks. You came up them crates like a cat, all but the last one."

She doesn't wait for him to argue.

"The lamp's Pell's. Rope-maker." Her voice moves along under the roof, toward the gap. "He leaves it lit every night, all night, swears it keeps the hemp thieves off. Fourteen years Da's had this stall and Pell's never once let it go out. Tonight he shuts up at the eighth bell, climbs on his step, and pinches it out with his fingers. Didn't even wet them. He swore and sucked his thumb all the way down." A short breath. "Then he shuts the loft hatch. He never shuts it in summer, the hemp sweats. Then off home, Rivington way, quick."

She stops, and he can hear her deciding whether to tell the next part.

"This afternoon a man came up the stair. Up from the water, not down off the bridge. He stood in Pell's door and talked to him low, then gave him something, and Pell bit it like I bit yours." Her voice drops. "Big hands. Knitted cap like yours, pulled down. Didn't buy any rope. Went back down the stair, and I never heard a boat go off, so it was waiting somewhere under there."

The boards creak as she shifts on the tubs.

"And your boat, yeah. I've heard it. Not every night. Once a week, maybe, since spring." Her voice goes flat when she says *spring*. "You don't hear the oars. They wrap them. All you hear is the water dripping off, plip, plip, and the boat bumping the footing. Every waterman on this river sings or swears. That lot do neither." She doesn't say anything for a moment. "I heard her once. The woman. On the stair. She talks soft, like she's putting a baby down. I put my head under the blanket."

Then, brisker, like she's selling him something:

"There's an iron ring on the footing under the first arch. That's where they tie up, I've seen the rope marks on it in the morning. You won't see it from the middle of the roof. Go to the back corner, the left one, by the crates. Put your head over the edge and look down past the drainpipe. You can see the ring and a bit of water either side." A pause. "Don't fall off. Da'd never believe I didn't push you."

The coin goes somewhere safe. He hears the rustle of cloth and a blanket being pulled up.

"I'm not asleep," Dace says to the boards. "Just so you know. I'm lying here with the gaff."

Then the stall is quiet. Out on the bridge Tobin is still calling the Lady to a crossing that has nearly emptied. Below, the Chionthar goes on talking to the stones. The back left corner of the roof is ten feet from his shoulder. It's about twenty past ten.

James breathes the words down through the boards: *if your da ever asks, I was a sack.*

Below him there's a snort, and the rustle of a blanket. "Sacks don't pay," Dace says. That's all she says.

He moves along the tar on his belly, one hand and then one knee, spreading his weight the way you cross a frozen pond. Nothing rocks this time. The roof gives a little under him and stays quiet. At the back left corner the drainpipe comes up out of the dark, cold and furred with old rust. He gets his cheek against the edge of the roof beside it and looks down.

The parapet falls away under him, and below it the Rock's footing. It's black stone, sheer, wet for the last few feet above the water. The ring is about twenty-five feet down and a little to his left, set into the stone just where the first great arch springs from the footing. It's iron, as big as a man's spread hand, and in what little light comes off the water it shows as a darker circle on dark stone. A frayed tail of old rope hangs from it, too short to be any use to anyone.

The current comes out from under the arch on his right and slides away to his left toward the harbour, smooth and fast, with little dimples on top where it curls round the footing. Anything tied to that ring would swing downstream and lie along the stone, out of the arch's mouth and in its shadow.

The dark line he saw at dusk is a ledge. It's a stone walk no wider than a boot is long, a foot above the water, slick with weed. It runs along the footing from the ring toward the bridge for about twenty feet, to where the last few steps of the stair come down out of the gap. Those he can just see, three or four treads shining wet, and then a small square landing at the water's edge. From a boat at the ring you could step onto the ledge, sidle along it with a hand on the wall, and come out at the bottom of the stair. From the top of the stair you could come down and never know a boat was there unless you looked along the footing. *She never looks at it,* Tobin said.

James fixes it in his eye. Then he settles in. His cap is down and his cheek is on the warm tar. One eye watches the stair head through the gap, the other the black under the arch, and he breathes the slow breath of a picket.

Down the bond he sends a light touch: *Where are you? Is the collar home yet?*

Nothing comes back. There's only the cottony nothing of a link stretched past where it reaches, like calling down a well with no water in it. Wherever the cat is, it's still in the Lower City, a long way off over the wall.

The bridge empties around him. A last cart goes by toward Rivington with its axle squealing. Two men pass the gap talking about a horse, and don't look at it. Back up the Crossing Tobin's patter goes on under his lamp, *find the Lady, find the Lady*, with longer gaps in it now. Nobody is there to hear it. The tar cools under James's chest. The river talks to the stones.

At a quarter to eleven he feels the edges of the face start to thin, like a coat going threadbare at the elbows. He puts a hand up and drags it down his jaw the way a man rubs himself awake, and mutters the words into his collar. The grey beard and the weathered nose settle back over him as before. To anyone counting, nothing has changed.

From under the boards, very low, comes Dace's voice: "Whatever that was, do it quieter."

The eleventh bell sounds from somewhere up the hill, then another, a beat behind, from farther off. Under the arch the black stays black.

A little before half past, the bond catches.

The first thing he gets is speed: cobbles, the Basilisk Gate's cold echo, bridge planks. Then the cat pushes the memory at him whole. A lantern bigger than the boy carrying it bobs along a street of narrow houses below the Counting House, and two pairs of legs walk in its light: small quick boots, and good shoes in no hurry. Nobody walks behind them. The cat checked more than once, from a wall-top and a doorway. The good shoes stop at a green door, and the door closes behind them. A minute later a candle comes into a window at the far end of the house, high up, burns for about as long as it takes to turn a key, and goes out. A candle lights in a different window, then that one goes out too.

*Home,* the cat says, in its way. *Both.*

Then it's on the crates behind him. It climbs them without rocking a single one, and he gets the faint feeling it intends him to notice that. It flows onto the roof and lies down against his hip, its ears pointed at the water.

Time goes slowly the way it does on a picket, a few breaths at a time. The cold comes up out of the river into the stone. Tobin's patter stops for a while, then starts again. It's getting on for twenty to midnight when the cat's ears go flat and then forward, both at once, toward the left. That's downstream, out past the end of the footing where the river opens toward the harbour.

James listens for what it heard.

He hears nothing. He listens until his ears ring with the river, and all the Chionthar gives him is its own voice, smooth water over stone. The cat's ears stay pinned forward, and the tip of its tail taps once on the tar.

One figure sits hunched at the oars, its shoulders wide and its head a round blot, still as a mooring post. The oars are shipped and lying along the gunwales. Beside him the cat has gone flat. Through the bond comes wet wool, tar, river-rot on old rope. Under that is something thin and sweetish that the cat doesn't like and can't put a name to. It doesn't come with a number.

Up the bridge, Tobin's patter stops in the middle of a word. A moment later James hears the scrape of a barrel being tipped back and the clatter of a lamp coming off its hook.

The midnight bell is about a quarter of an hour off.
